SCHOOL ROOM · THE CLUBS · 45 CARDS · AGES 3–12

The Clubs — every card opens a hobby.

Forty-five after-school clubs on forty-five cards: art, music, dance and thirteen more for the youngest members, then chess, coding, fencing and the rest for ages 6 and up. Every card prints the two skills its club trains — Aim & Focus, Calm & Wellbeing, Measure & Create — every club has its own short page, its own lesson and a printable twin, and the room was built for choosing: try one, keep one, grow one.

Open the club shelves ↓The printable set ↗
HOW THIS ROOM WORKS

Pick a club. Read its skills. Try it this week.

Every card in this deck does two jobs: it names one club and it prints the two skills that club trains, right under the picture. The room splits by age the way the school does: the first shelf holds the fifteen clubs made for the youngest members — tagged Ages 3+ — and the second shelf holds the thirty clubs for older members, tagged Ages 6+. When one club becomes a favorite, its lesson page carries the full teaching — what the club is, what the skills secretly train, the parent script, the questions to ask — and the library page holds the printable twin with a download button.

A word on safety, because it matters here: some clubs are coach clubs. Fencing and archery always run with a trained coach and proper equipment — their pages say so — and swimming, climbing and horse riding belong wherever trained adults and the right gear are standard. The card starts the hobby; the grown-ups keep it safe.

THE YOUNG CLUB SHELF · AGES 3+

Fifteen clubs for the youngest members.

Art, music, dance, sports, drama, gardening, cooking, ballet, yoga, swimming, reading, crafts, drawing, baking and singing — the fifteen clubs that work from age three, in the order the school recommends trying them. Tap any card to open its short page.

Thirty clubs for ages 6 and up.

From archery to volunteering — the strategy clubs, the workshop clubs, the coach-led sports and the word clubs. Younger members wait for these; the skills are worth the wait.

GAMES THE CLUBS PLAY

Warm-ups from the games shelf.

Club time and game time trade places all afternoon, and the school’s games shelf holds the rules for the warm-ups every club borrows: Animal Walks opens dance, drama and yoga bodies, Musical Statues trains the freeze every performance needs, Relay Race is sports club’s favorite drill, Obstacle Course is gymnastics night at home, and Simon Says sharpens the listening every club runs on. Full rules on every page.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Art — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the art club habit at home: a small setup, one invitation to paint, and a closing ritual that makes the child want to come back tomorrow.

What is this?

Art club is regular, unstructured making time — paint, crayons, glue and paper, offered so often it stops being an event and becomes a habit. The club’s printed skills are Painting & Creativity: the hand learns control while the mind learns to invent.

What does it mean?

A regular art session teaches process over product: the painting matters less than the deciding, testing and changing that happens on the way. Children who choose their own colors and subjects practice independence on paper.

What does the child need to know?

Paper, paints or crayons, a surface that can survive drips, and five unbothered minutes. An old shirt as a smock and a wet cloth within reach prevent most cleanup stress.

Why this matters

Open-ended art builds fine-motor control, decision-making and creative confidence — and it is the cheapest, most repeatable club a family can run. A child who paints weekly talks more, plans more and worries less.

What it teaches

Grip strength, color choice and naming, planning ahead, self-expression, and the tidy-up ritual that ends every real studio session.

Words to learn

paintpalettebrushgallerycreatemixframemasterpiece

Say this to your child

“"Welcome to art club! Here is your paper, here are your colors, and here is the best rule of all: whatever you make is right. I am going to paint too — show me how it is done."”

Step by step

  1. Cover the table, lay out paper and no more than three paint colors — small choices are easier choices.
  2. Say the club’s one rule: in art club, whatever you make is right.
  3. Paint alongside for the first minutes without correcting — copy the child’s strokes instead.
  4. Ask process questions: which color comes next? what is the brush doing?
  5. End with the hanging ceremony: the painting goes up on the wall or fridge, the artist chooses the spot, and the room applauds.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the painter stands at a real easel with a palette in hand — easels keep paintings upright and visible, which is why art classrooms use them, and why the wall next to the kitchen table works just as well.

Ask your child

"What did you paint first?" "Which color was the best surprise?" "Where should this painting hang?" "What will tomorrow’s painting need?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may narrate every stroke, paint over a finished area with total confidence, or declare the whole sheet one color by the end — all three are legitimate art-club sessions.

Out in the real world

Illustrators, house painters, sign makers and animators all started with a brush and a sheet of paper at a kitchen table. The habit of making is the job interview.

Try it together

Musical paint: one sheet per person, paint while the song plays, and when it stops everyone slides one seat to the left to add to someone else’s painting. Collaborative art, no arguments.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is art club’s one rule?" (whatever you make is right) "Name the three things we set up." (paper, colors, cover) "What happens to a finished painting?" (it hangs)

This lesson pairs with the Art flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Music — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the music club habit: one steady beat, a family echo game, and permission for every pot in the cupboard to be an instrument for ten minutes.

What is this?

Music club is regular sound play — clapping, singing, kitchen drums — where the goal is a felt beat, not a performance. The card’s printed skills are Rhythm & Sound: the steady pulse underneath music and the many ways things can vibrate.

What does it mean?

Keeping a steady beat trains the same timing the body uses for walking, cutting and swinging. Echo games train listening memory — hearing a pattern and holding it in the head is early math wearing a song’s clothes.

What does the child need to know?

Two clapping hands, a pot and a wooden spoon, and one song everybody likes. A shaker (rice in a sealed bottle) adds a second voice to the family band.

Why this matters

Rhythm play is one of the strongest predictors of early reading — syllables live on beats. Music sessions also teach turn-taking naturally: you play, then I play.

What it teaches

Steady-beat keeping, listening memory, loud/soft and fast/slow contrast words, turn-taking, and the confidence that comes from making a sound nobody stops.

Words to learn

beatrhythmloudsoftfastslowechoshakertempo

Say this to your child

“"Music club is open! First we find the beat — clap with me, one two one two. Now you are the leader, I will echo everything you play. Ready?"”

Step by step

  1. Clap the steady beat while a song plays — pat knees if clapping is too loud.
  2. Play echo claps: three-beat patterns, child echoes, then swap leader roles.
  3. Explore loud and soft with the pot drum: thunder hands, mouse hands.
  4. March the beat around the room — big steps for loud, tiptoes for soft.
  5. Finish with one song sung together, then one minute of silence to hear the difference.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the player’s fingers spread across a small keyboard — pianos show the pattern of music visually, low notes on the left walking down, high on the right climbing up.

Ask your child

"Is this music loud or soft?" "Can your feet keep the beat?" "What did my pattern sound like?" "What in this kitchen could join the band?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may keep a beat with surprising accuracy, invent a two-note song with real words in it, or drum on every surface in the house — the last one is called practice.

Out in the real world

Musicians, dancers, surgeons and baristas all rely on rhythm — steady timing is the hidden skill behind espresso shots and heartbeats alike.

Try it together

Kitchen orchestra: assign every player one object (pot, shaker, spoon-glass), pick a steady beat, and conduct loud and soft with big and small hand waves. The conductor gets to end the piece with a fist — silence at last.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we call the steady pulse?" (the beat) "Show me soft hands on the drum." "What happens when I clap a pattern?" (we echo it back)

This lesson pairs with the Music flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Dance — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the dance club habit: one song, one open floor, and games that teach the body to say happy, sleepy and gigantic without a single word.

What is this?

Dance club is movement with feeling attached — free dancing, freeze games and pretend-the-floor-is games that teach the body to express what the face is thinking. The card’s printed skills are Movement & Expression: controlled motion plus the story inside it.

What does it mean?

Dancing to different tempos trains listening with the whole body. Holding a freeze trains real control — stopping is harder than going, and mastering the stop is where the discipline hides.

What does the child need to know?

An open patch of floor, one playlist with a fast song, a slow song and a silly song. Socks that slide make everything better; nothing else is required.

Why this matters

Dance builds coordination, balance and listening — and it gives big feelings a safe exit. A child who can dance their frustration out often needs fewer words for it later.

What it teaches

Body control, balance, tempo listening, emotional expression, spatial awareness (dancing without collisions is a real skill), and performance courage.

Words to learn

dancefreezetempoleapspintiptoeexpressstagebow

Say this to your child

“"Dance club is open! First we warm up every part of us... now DANCE! When the music stops, freeze like a statue. Ready — and show me what happy feet look like!"”

Step by step

  1. Warm up every part: roll shoulders, wiggle hips, shake hands like jelly.
  2. Free dance to the fast song — the only rule is keep moving.
  3. Freeze dance: when the music stops, the statue holds until it returns.
  4. Emotion walk: dance happy, dance sleepy, dance like a giant, dance like the floor is lava.
  5. Slow-motion dance to the quiet song, then take a bow — every show ends with one.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the dancer is caught mid-leap with both arms open — dancing is the only sport where the audience can see the music, which is what the leap is doing.

Ask your child

"Show me sleepy dancing." "Which was harder — freezing or dancing?" "What does a giant’s dance look like?" "How do dancers end a show?" (a bow)

What your child can say or do

Your child may invent a signature move within one song, demand the freeze song four times, or choreograph the pets — audiences may vary, enthusiasm never does.

Out in the real world

Dancers, figure skaters, cheerleaders and wedding guests all speak this language — moving to music is a skill the whole species shares.

Try it together

Follow the leader dance: the leader invents one move per verse, everyone copies, then the next dancer leads. Four leaders later, the family has invented a whole dance.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do when the music stops?" (freeze) "Show me a slow-motion dance move." "How does every show end?" (a bow)

This lesson pairs with the Dance flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Sports — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the sports club habit at home: cooperative ball games first, competition gently later, and the post-game handshake from day one.

What is this?

Sports club is regular moving-and-playing-together time — ball passes, relay games, chase games — where the printed skills are Teamwork & Fitness: the body gets stronger and the group gets friendlier at the same time.

What does it mean?

Passing before shooting teaches the deepest sports habit: looking for your teammate. Cooperative games keep beginners in the club; competition is fun only after the group already trusts itself.

What does the child need to know?

One soft ball, a little space, and two or more players. Chairs make excellent goals, socks make excellent balls, and the handshake needs nothing at all.

Why this matters

Team games build coordination, stamina and the social engine — turn-taking, encouragement, and losing without collapsing. Fitness at this age is play that happens to be exercise.

What it teaches

Gross-motor control, throwing and catching accuracy, turn-taking, encouragement words, and the emotional equipment for winning and losing small games.

Words to learn

teampassgoalrallyfair playcheerhandshakecoach

Say this to your child

“"Sports club practice starts now! First we warm up like animals... now pass the ball and count with me — one, two, three! Every goal gets a cheer for everybody. Here we go!"”

Step by step

  1. Warm up with animal laps around the space — bear, crab, bunny.
  2. Pass-and-count: roll or throw the ball back and forth, counting catches out loud to ten.
  3. Add the moving part: after each pass, both players switch spots.
  4. Play two-goal soccer with chairs; every goal earns a team cheer for BOTH players.
  5. Close with the handshake ritual — game over, hands out, good game — the habit that outlasts every score.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the player holds the ball with both hands and a grin — possession matters less than the joy, which is why the grin is part of the uniform.

Ask your child

"What do we say after every game?" (good game) "How do we pass so our teammate catches it?" (gently, to their hands) "Who else could join our team?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may invent elaborate team names and uniforms, keep score for both sides generously, or shake hands with the goalposts — sportsmanship has many styles.

Out in the real world

Every team sport on Earth runs on the pass-first habit — basketball assists, soccer through-balls, relay batons. The living room is where it starts.

Try it together

Cooperative kickball: the whole family kicks in a circle, and the team score is how many kicks happen before the ball stops. The record exists only to be broken together.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name one way to be a good teammate." (pass, cheer, include) "What do we do after every game?" (shake hands, good game) "Show me your warm-up animal."

This lesson pairs with the Sports flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Drama — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the drama club habit: a warm-up body, a borrowed character, and the discovery that speaking in someone else’s voice is the easiest way to find your own.

What is this?

Drama club is pretend with structure — characters, voices, and small stories performed for anyone in the room. The card’s printed skills are Stories & Confidence: inventing the tale and standing up while telling it.

What does it mean?

Playing a character lets a shy child say bold things safely — the dragon says what the child is not ready to. Inventing stories trains sequencing (first, then, suddenly) which is the skeleton of every school essay later.

What does the child need to know?

A corner that can be a stage, three random objects as story props, and an audience of one or more. Costumes are optional; a hat changes everything.

Why this matters

Drama builds language, sequencing, empathy (every character has feelings to manage) and the specific courage of being watched. It is the club where shy children regularly become loud ones.

What it teaches

Story sequencing, voice control, emotional vocabulary, eye contact with an audience, improvisation (a story that bends when a prop changes), and stage courage.

Words to learn

characterscenestageaudiencecostumeactbowvoicestory

Say this to your child

“"Drama club is open! Warm up your walking... now pick your character — who are you today? Give them a voice. Here are three mystery props: the story must use all three!"”

Step by step

  1. Warm up the body: walk like a robot, glide like a cat, stomp like a giant.
  2. Pick the character: name, voice, and the walk that goes with it.
  3. Open the story suitcase — three objects — and build the story around them.
  4. Perform the one-scene show for the audience; the audience claps between scenes.
  5. Take the bow together — performers and audience — then swap roles so every actor gets a turn and every audience gets a turn too.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the actor gestures with an open hand mid-story — the gesture is doing the words’ job, which is exactly what actors mean by showing, not telling.

Ask your child

"What is your character’s name?" "How does your character feel right now?" "What happens when the spoon arrives in the story?" "How does an actor end the show?" (with a bow)

What your child can say or do

Your child may stay in character through dinner, give the audience speaking roles, or discover the microphone-power of the hairbrush — every theater has one.

Out in the real world

Actors, teachers, lawyers and YouTubers all live on this skill: standing in front of people and carrying a story. The living-room stage is the first one.

Try it together

The interview show: one player is a celebrity (a cat, an astronaut, a pancake chef), the other is the reporter with five questions. Switch roles after the commercials.

Understanding check

Ask: "What three things does a character need?" (a name, a voice, a walk) "What do we do with the story suitcase?" (use all three props) "How do we end a show?" (bow together)

This lesson pairs with the Drama flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Gardening — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the gardening club habit: one clear-cup bean, one watering schedule the child owns, and a diary that turns waiting into watching.

What is this?

Gardening club is regular plant care — planting, watering, watching, harvesting — where the printed skills are Nature & Care: knowing living things and keeping them alive. It is the only club where a day off literally shows on the plant.

What does it mean?

Tending a plant teaches cause and effect on a delay — water today, sprout next week — which is the deepest lesson in responsibility. Naming the plant makes the care real; children water named plants far more reliably than pots.

What does the child need to know?

Dried beans, a clear cup, a little potting soil, a spray bottle a small hand can press, and a sunny windowsill. Everything else is decoration.

Why this matters

Gardening builds patience, observation and the caretaker identity — the child becomes the person something depends on. It also quietly teaches where food starts, which reshapes lunch conversations.

What it teaches

Patience and delayed reward, observation over days, responsibility routines, plant vocabulary, and the gentle-touch skills that come with handling seedlings.

Words to learn

seedsproutrootsoilwatersunlightgrowshootleaf

Say this to your child

“"Gardening club opens with one bean! We tuck it in against the cup wall so we can watch its roots grow. Two sprays of water every morning — that is our promise. What is our plant’s name?"”

Step by step

  1. Press the bean against the inside wall of the clear cup, wrapped in a little soil — the root will be visible.
  2. Water together: two sprays, same time every morning.
  3. Give the plant a name and a spot where the child sees it at breakfast.
  4. Keep the sprout diary: one drawing every two days, dated like a scientist’s log.
  5. Celebrate the first root, the first shoot, and the first true leaf — three parties per bean.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the gardener waters a seedling already standing in its pot — the card shows the middle of the story: the sprout is proof the early care happened.

Ask your child

"What does our plant need every morning?" (water) "Where do plants get their food?" (sunlight — they cook it themselves) "What changed since yesterday?" "What will the sprout do next?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may check the cup six times a morning, narrate to the plant by name, or line up a second and third bean for siblings — gardeners always expand.

Out in the real world

Farmers, florists, botanists and park keepers all run on plant care. The windowsill bean is the smallest farm in the world and runs on the same rules.

Try it together

Grow-a-sentence: each morning the child adds one word to a sentence taped beside the plant — our bean is... growing... tall... — the sentence grows with the plant.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are our two jobs?" (water and watch) "What does the plant need besides water?" (sun) "What comes first, root or shoot?" (the root)

This lesson pairs with the Gardening flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Cooking — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the cooking club habit: the child wears the apron and makes the choices, the grown-up owns the heat, and one simple dish becomes the family’s Tuesday classic.

What is this?

Cooking club is regular kitchen time with real jobs — pouring, stirring, spreading, tearing — where the printed skills are Food & Independence: knowing what goes into food and making some of it yourself.

What does it mean?

Cooking is the most useful math and science lab in the house: measuring is fractions, cooking is chemistry, and eating the result is the best feedback loop ever designed. Choosing the menu trains decision-making with immediate, delicious consequences.

What does the child need to know?

A stable chair or learning tower, one mixing bowl, child-safe tools (a butter knife genuinely cuts a banana), ingredients for one simple dish, and a hand-wash station. Heat stays with the grown-up.

Why this matters

Children who cook eat braver — they try what they made. Kitchen jobs also build sequencing, measuring, patience while things bake, and the pride of feeding the family.

What it teaches

Sequencing and following steps, measuring and counting, hand strength (stirring thick batter is a workout), kitchen safety habits, and tasting vocabulary (salty, sour, crunchy).

Words to learn

chefrecipemixstirpourmeasurebaketasteingredient

Say this to your child

“"Cooking club is open — tonight YOU are the chef and I am your helper. Wash those hands, chef! First we read the recipe. Which ingredient goes in first?"”

Step by step

  1. Wash hands and tie the apron — the uniform makes it official.
  2. Read the recipe out loud and count the ingredients together.
  3. Assign the child the safe jobs: measuring, pouring, stirring, arranging.
  4. Chef decides: more cheese or less? round shapes or stars? The helper executes.
  5. Taste test at the end with real words — what is salty, what is sweet — then the chef signs off the dish with a name.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the cook’s whisk stands tall in a big bowl with the apron already on — the whisk and apron are the two tools that say this kitchen belongs to the chef today.

Ask your child

"What does the chef do first?" (wash hands) "What is our helper’s job?" (the oven — heat is the grown-up’s) "What does our dish taste like?" "What should we cook next week?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may plate the dish like a restaurant, invent a dish name with its own song, or set a pretend menu for tomorrow — chefs with one success book the next night immediately.

Out in the real world

Chefs, bakers, food scientists and dietitians all started by stirring something at a counter beside a grown-up. Every restaurant was once a kitchen with a chair in it.

Try it together

Restaurant night: the child writes (or draws) the menu, takes the family’s orders with a notepad, and the family eats whatever the chef assembled. Tips are paid in bedtime stories.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who washes hands in cooking club?" (everybody, first) "Name your job tonight." (measure, pour, stir...) "What does the grown-up own?" (the heat and the oven)

This lesson pairs with the Cooking flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Ballet — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the ballet club habit: five beginner positions in miniature, the hot-soup arms, and a slow song that turns the hallway into a stage.

What is this?

Ballet club is gentle, structured movement — positions, posture and slow controlled motion — where the printed skills are Balance & Grace: steady holds and soft, deliberate moves. Ballet is the club where standing still is a real achievement.

What does it mean?

Ballet trains the body’s quiet muscles — posture, turnout, pointed toes — and the mind’s patience: slow counts feel long at four years old. Learning French step names adds the pleasure of secret vocabulary.

What does the child need to know?

Bare feet or soft shoes, a strip of clear floor, and one slow classical or gentle song. A full-length mirror helps but a window reflection works fine.

Why this matters

Ballet builds posture, balance and body control better than almost any activity — and it teaches practice culture: tiny movements repeated until they look easy. It is also the gateway vocabulary behind figure skating, gymnastics and every movie dance scene.

What it teaches

Balance on one foot, posture muscles, slow-motion control, listening to counts, following multi-part instructions, and performance calm.

Words to learn

first positionpliétiptoearabesquebalancegracebowstage

Say this to your child

“"Ballet club is open! Heels together, toes out — first position. Now carry the hot soup on your arm and walk on tiptoes... no spills! Slow dancers are the strongest dancers."”

Step by step

  1. Warm up: roll the shoulders, point and flex the feet ten times.
  2. First position: heels together, toes out — hold for a slow count of five.
  3. Hot-soup arms: one arm round and forward, walking on tiptoes without spilling.
  4. The slow dance: one gentle song, moving only in slow motion, ending in a held balance.
  5. The ballet bow: one foot behind, a small dip, head up — every class ends with one.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the dancer’s standing leg is straight and strong while the other points back in arabesque — the lift looks effortless because every muscle underneath is working.

Ask your child

"Show me first position." "How do we walk so the soup never spills?" (slow, tiptoes) "Why do dancers practice so slowly?" (control is the skill) "How does class end?" (a bow)

What your child can say or do

Your child may practice positions in the supermarket line, teach the family the hot-soup arms, or demand the slow song twice — ballerinas know their program.

Out in the real world

Ballet training hides inside figure skating, gymnastics, cheerleading and every musical — choreographers borrow its positions the way chefs borrow the knife grip.

Try it together

Swan lake in the hallway: one slow song, arms as wings, one grand walk the length of the hall, one held balance, one bow. Repeat until the audience demands an encore.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are first position’s feet doing?" (heels together, toes out) "What do the arms carry?" (the hot soup) "Name a ballet skill that is slow." (tiptoe walk, arabesque)

This lesson pairs with the Ballet flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Yoga — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the yoga club habit: three poses a child can hold, breath games that disguise deep breathing as animal noises, and one quiet minute that ends every session.

What is this?

Yoga club is regular slow-stretching and breathing time, on a mat or a rug, where the printed skills are Calm & Wellbeing: a body that can settle and a mood that follows. It is the club with the lowest volume and the highest patience.

What does it mean?

Yoga teaches interoception — noticing what the body feels — through poses that are fun to name. The breathing games are real regulation tools in costume: a lion’s roar empties the lungs, a snake’s hiss slows the exhale.

What does the child need to know?

A rug or mat, enough floor to stretch both ways, and a voice kept low on purpose. Loose clothes help; nothing else is needed.

Why this matters

Yoga gives children the first tools of self-regulation: slow breath, still body, named feeling. Practiced at bedtime it shortens the trip to sleep; practiced at high-energy moments it becomes a reset the child can run alone.

What it teaches

Balance and flexibility, breath control, body awareness, stillness stamina, and the emotional habit of noticing feelings without being flooded by them.

Words to learn

posebreathestretchbalancecalmrootstallgentlerest

Say this to your child

“"Yoga club is open — soft voices on the mat. First the snake breath: hiiissss... now tree pose, roots down, branches up. How still can our tree stand?"”

Step by step

  1. Begin with three animal breaths: snake hiss, lion roar, bunny sniffs.
  2. Tree pose: one foot pressed to the standing leg, roots down, branches up — hold for three breaths.
  3. The slow fold: reach for the toes, hang there, sway like a windblown tree.
  4. Bridge or cat-cow, whichever the mat allows, moving with the breath.
  5. Close with the listening minute: lying still, eyes closed, counting the quiet sounds — the club’s signature ending.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the yogi stands in tree pose with palms together over the head — the hands-up shape is the branches, and the stillness is the whole exercise.

Ask your child

"Which breath is longest — snake, lion or bunny?" "Show me your tree." "What did you hear in the listening minute?" "When could yoga help at home?" (before bed, after big feelings)

What your child can say or do

Your child may invent new poses named after the pets, run the snake breath to calm a sibling, or request the listening minute at bedtime — the habit migrates.

Out in the real world

Athletes, dancers and surgeons use breath control; every gym class and every calming corner in every school borrows yoga’s poses and breathing.

Try it together

Pose cards face down: draw a card, hold the pose for three breaths, then teach it to the next player. Five cards make a full class — the child as teacher, the family as students.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me tree pose." "Which animal breath empties the lungs biggest?" (lion) "What ends every yoga club?" (the listening minute)

This lesson pairs with the Yoga flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Swimming — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the swimming club habit: the safety recital before every visit, the water games that make letting go of the wall feel like a game, and the patience the pool asks for.

What is this?

Swimming club is regular pool time with a safety spine — bubbles, floats, kicks and the rules that never bend. The card’s printed skills are Confidence & Safety: comfort in the water and the rules that keep it safe.

What does it mean?

The water rules (never alone, walk on the deck, feet first) must be rehearsed out loud until they are automatic — reciting them is part of the lesson, not a formality. Confidence grows from small wins: a bubble, a glide, a kick to the wall.

What does the child need to know?

A pool with a lifeguard, a grown-up within arm’s reach at all times, a swimsuit that stays put, and goggles if they help the child open their eyes underwater. Armbands only if the pool recommends them.

Why this matters

Swimming is the one sport that is also a life skill — the earlier the habit of rules-plus-fun is built, the safer every water year after. Pool sessions also build breath control, full-body strength and nerve.

What it teaches

Breath control (blowing bubbles), leg strength, floating trust, rule memory, and the emotional arc from clinging to the wall to pushing off it.

Words to learn

poolbubblesfloatkickgoggleslifeguarddeckglide

Say this to your child

“"Swimming club starts on the steps — rules first! Never alone, walk on the deck, grown-up watching. Now let’s blow bubbles... chin in the water, brrr — how many bubbles did we make?"”

Step by step

  1. On the deck, before entering: recite the three rules together — never alone, walk by the pool, a grown-up always watching.
  2. Enter by the steps and sit on the shallow step — the water gets a turn to say hello.
  3. Bubble game: chin in, blow bubbles, count them, come up grinning.
  4. Wall kicks: hold the edge, kick straight legs, make the water splash loud.
  5. Glide to the grown-up: one push from the step into open arms — two steps further each visit, celebrated every time.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the goggles rest UP on the forehead between swims — swimmers spend real time on the deck too, and the card shows the club’s honest rhythm: swim, rest, repeat.

Ask your child

"What are the three water rules?" "How do we get INTO the pool?" (steps, slowly) "What do we do at the wall?" (kick!) "Who is always watching?" (the grown-up, the lifeguard)

What your child can say or do

Your child may recite the rules to strangers at the pool (excellent), refuse to leave at the end (typical), or invent a bubble-counting championship — the pool builds regulars fast.

Out in the real world

Swim teachers, lifeguards, marine biologists and every summer vacation run on this skill. The wall-kick stage is where every swimmer in history started.

Try it together

Treasury of steps: place three sinking toys on the shallow step, the child retrieves one per turn with a grown-up’s hand nearby — underwater reaching is the bravery ladder’s first rung.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the three water rules." "Show me how we enter the pool." "What do swimmers blow?" (bubbles) "When can we swim alone?" (never — always a grown-up watching)

This lesson pairs with the Swimming flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Reading — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the reading club habit: the child picks the book, the grown-up brings the voices, and prediction turns every page turn into a game.

What is this?

Reading club is a daily story appointment — same cushion, same ten minutes, book chosen by the child. The card’s printed skills are Imagine & Learn: the pictures the mind builds and the facts it collects along the way.

What does it mean?

Choice is the engine: children who pick their own books read longer and ask to re-read, and re-reading is where the real learning hides — the second pass notices everything the first missed. Predicting the next page trains comprehension before the words are even decoded.

What does the child need to know?

A book basket with three to five choices, a reading spot with the good light, and voices: one for the bear, one for the wind, one whisper for the secret pages.

Why this matters

Daily reading is the single highest-leverage habit in early childhood — vocabulary, attention, empathy and school readiness all ride on it. The ritual matters as much as the book: same time, same spot, same voices.

What it teaches

Vocabulary growth, story sequencing, prediction skills, listening stamina, print awareness (text runs left to right, pages turn one way), and the book-love that outlasts the lesson.

Words to learn

storypagepredictcharacterbeginningendlibraryfavoritechapter

Say this to your child

“"Reading club! Bring me the basket — you pick today’s book. Let’s guess from the cover: what happens? ... Now listen to the bear’s voice. And STOP — what happens next?"”

Step by step

  1. The basket comes out; the child chooses today’s book with full ceremony.
  2. Read the cover: title, author, and a guess from the picture of what happens.
  3. Read with voices — slow down at the good parts, pause before the turn.
  4. Play pause-and-predict: stop one page early and let everyone guess the ending.
  5. Close with the re-read offer: same book again is ALWAYS allowed — favorites are how readers are made.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the book is open to a castle page and held toward the viewer — the picture inside the book is doing its job: the reader is already inside the story.

Ask your child

"What do you think happens next?" "Which voice should the wolf have?" "Who was your favorite character?" "Should we read it again tomorrow?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may memorize whole pages and recite them (real reading’s first draft), demand the same book for two weeks (excellent), or read to the pets — audiences of fur are traditional.

Out in the real world

Authors, librarians, teachers and podcasters all live on stories read aloud first. Every big reader started in a lap with a book they chose themselves.

Try it together

Story detectives: after the book, three quick questions — who, what happened first, what changed? Three answers and the detective badge is earned for the day.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who chooses the book in reading club?" (the reader) "What do we do at the pause?" (predict) "How long does club last?" (ten minutes — every day)

This lesson pairs with the Reading flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Crafts — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the crafts club habit: one box of rescued materials, one project with a real finish line, and the maker’s rule that the second version is always allowed.

What is this?

Crafts club is building time from reclaimed stuff — tubes, boxes, fabric scraps, buttons — where the printed skills are Make & Explore: constructing the idea and trying variations without fear.

What does it mean?

Craft materials with no single right answer teach divergent thinking: a tube is a rocket, then an owl, then a megaphone. The loop — choose, build, test, improve — is engineering in miniature with glue instead of code.

What does the child need to know?

A dedicated box: cardboard tubes, clean cartons, paper scraps, tape, a glue stick, safety scissors, stickers and string. The box gets refilled by the household itself, which is the best part.

Why this matters

Crafts build fine-motor control, planning, and the specific confidence of having MADE something from nothing. A weekly session also cleans the recycling bin, which the planet appreciates.

What it teaches

Fine-motor precision, spatial planning (which piece goes where), material problem-solving, creative reuse, and project completion — finishing is a trainable muscle.

Words to learn

craftmaterialsscrapsbuildimprovecollagetexturerecycle

Say this to your child

“"Crafts club! Bring the box — today the zoo opens at four. Sort your materials... now build your first animal. What is it? What should its name be? The audience is coming!"”

Step by step

  1. Open the craft box together and sort by type — paper here, tubes there.
  2. Announce the project with a deadline: the tube zoo opens at four o’clock.
  3. Build each animal: tube body, paper ears, sticker eyes, a name for everyone.
  4. The improve round: builders may add one upgrade to any animal before opening.
  5. Grand opening: the shelf becomes the zoo, every keeper presents their animal, and the audience votes for Best Use of a Bottle Cap.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the maker holds scissors, a glue stick and a half-built paper house — three tools, one project underway: the card is always photographed in the middle of making, never after.

Ask your child

"What could this tube become?" "Which part is hardest to stick?" (answer it together) "What would make it better?" "Where does the finished piece live?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may build a whole habitat, tape three boxes into a robot the size of the cat, or give every animal a birthday — craft clubs have spin-offs.

Out in the real world

Engineers, architects, prop makers and toy designers all started by building animals from tubes. The box of scraps is a prototype studio.

Try it together

Mystery build: each player grabs three random items from the box blind — must build something that uses all three. The reveal is half comedy, half engineering.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where do our materials come from?" (the box, rescued things) "Name the maker’s loop." (choose, build, improve) "What happens at four o’clock?" (the zoo opens)

This lesson pairs with the Crafts flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Drawing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the drawing club habit: a short look-first exercise, a silly game that removes the fear, and one real object drawn together on the same page.

What is this?

Drawing club is regular pencil time with the eyes in charge — look-then-draw games, shape-first sketches and one shared drawing per session. The card’s printed skills are See & Create: careful looking followed by brave making.

What does it mean?

Drawing what the eyes actually see — not the memory of a thing — is the club’s core skill, and it is trained with games: the blind contour removes perfectionism by making results hilarious on purpose. Shapes first, details later is how every artist, animator and police sketch artist works.

What does the child need to know?

Paper, one pencil, one real object to look at (an apple, a shoe, the family pet if it holds still), and a wall ready to become the gallery. Erasers optional — this club rewards second tries, not perfect firsts.

Why this matters

Drawing builds observation, fine-motor control and patience — and it feeds every other skill on the shelf: science diagrams, story maps, math shapes. A weekly look-then-draw habit quietly upgrades how the child sees everything.

What it teaches

Observation (shape, size, position), fine-motor control, part-to-whole thinking, creative confidence, and the studio habit of dating and keeping work.

Words to learn

sketchoutlineshapedetailgalleryobserveartistdateframe

Say this to your child

“"Drawing club! First we LOOK — ten quiet seconds at our apple... now tell me every shape you see. Shapes first, details later. Ready, artists? And now... blind contour — eyes on the apple, NEVER the paper!"”

Step by step

  1. Warm up the eyes: study the object for ten silent seconds, then describe it out loud — shapes, sizes, surprises.
  2. Draw it together, shapes first: big forms before small details, both drawing on the same sheet.
  3. Play the blind contour: one hand, eyes on the object only, the paper’s result is guaranteed ridiculous — and the room guarantees the laugh.
  4. Draw it a second time with full freedom — the second drawing is always better, which teaches the deepest lesson in the club.
  5. Date both drawings and hang the best one in the gallery; the wall grows weekly.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the sketch pad shows a house built from a square and a triangle — the card itself demonstrates the club’s method: every picture starts from shapes.

Ask your child

"What shapes does our object hide?" "Was the second drawing better? Why?" "What did the blind contour teach us?" (drawing is allowed to be silly) "What should we draw next week?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may draw the object from memory instead of looking (a fine first draft), label everything with words, or start a gallery waiting list for the family cat.

Out in the real world

Animators, architects, botanists and detectives all draw what they see. The shape-first method is the same one used in art schools and police sketchrooms.

Try it together

Drawing telephone: one player draws a shape, the next adds one thing, the next one more — five turns later the drawing gets titled by the last player, who has no idea what happened.

Understanding check

Ask: "What comes first — shapes or details?" (shapes) "How long do we look before drawing?" (ten seconds) "What do we write on the back?" (the date — artists always date)

This lesson pairs with the Drawing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Baking — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the baking club habit: the child becomes the measurer, the recipe becomes a sequence to follow, and the waiting-for-the-oven problem gets a game.

What is this?

Baking club is recipe-following time in the kitchen — measuring, pouring, mixing — where the printed skills are Measure & Create: exact amounts and the transformation they become. Baking is cooking’s precise sibling: the recipe rules here.

What does it mean?

Leveling a cup teaches a rare thing at this age: exactness matters, and it is achievable. The recipe’s order (dry first? wet first?) is real sequencing practice, and the oven’s timer is the club’s built-in patience lesson.

What does the child need to know?

A recipe with six or fewer steps, measuring cups and spoons, one big bowl, a baking tray, and a grown-up who owns the oven from start to finish. Aprons on; flour clouds expected.

Why this matters

Baking builds measuring confidence (early math), sequence-following (early reading), and kitchen science curiosity — why did the dough rise? It also ends with the highest reward-to-effort ratio of any club: something warm to share.

What it teaches

Measuring and leveling, counting scoops, sequencing steps, fine-motor pouring, oven patience, and sharing the finished tray with actual guests.

Words to learn

measurelevelcupteaspoondoughoventimerbatchshare

Say this to your child

“"Baking club! Recipe first — how many ingredients? Now you scoop and I level: flat like snow. One cup, two teaspoons... stir, stir, stir. And the timer is YOURS, chef: how many minutes?"”

Step by step

  1. Read the recipe together and count the ingredients on the counter.
  2. Measure one: the child scoops, you level with the back of a knife — flat tops every time.
  3. Pour and stir in order, narrating the sequence: first the flour, then this, then that.
  4. The tray goes to the grown-up and the oven — the child sets the timer and owns the countdown.
  5. While it bakes, play the prediction game: what will change? color? size? smell? Then the tray cools, and the club tastes and votes on the best bite.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the baker’s tray holds six frosted cupcakes and two cookies — more than one person could eat, which is the point: baking is the club that feeds other people.

Ask your child

"What does the back of the knife do?" (levels the cup) "What does the oven change?" (dough becomes cake — heat transforms) "Who owns the timer?" (the chef) "Who gets the first taste?" (the baker chooses — then shares)

What your child can say or do

Your child may level every cup in the house with intense seriousness, check the oven window nine times, or schedule the next batch before the first has cooled.

Out in the real world

Bakers, pastry chefs and food scientists live by measured grams and exact temperatures — and every one of them started by leveling one cup beside a grown-up.

Try it together

Muffin-count math: the tray has twelve cups — if we fill six, how many are empty? Count together, fill together, and the answer is warm in twenty minutes.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do to the cup after scooping?" (level it flat) "Who opens the oven?" (the grown-up) "What does baking teach that frying does not?" (exact measuring matters)

This lesson pairs with the Baking flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Singing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the singing club habit: a hum to warm up, echo games that make singing a conversation, and one song the child owns well enough to teach the family.

What is this?

Singing club is regular voice time — warm-ups, echo songs, and one favorite song carried all the way through. The card’s printed skills are Voice & Confidence: the sound itself and the nerve to let it out loud.

What does it mean?

Singing is speaking with the volume and shape turned up — the same muscles, the same words. Echo games remove performance pressure by making every line a copy; high-and-low play teaches that the voice is an instrument with settings.

What does the child need to know?

A room where loud is allowed, one song the family knows, and a pretend microphone (hairbrush, spoon) for the solo moments. No instrument required — the voice ships with the child.

Why this matters

Singing builds language (melody makes words stick), breath control, pitch listening and stage nerve. It is also the most portable club in the school: cars, bathtubs and supermarket lines all become stages.

What it teaches

Pitch matching, breath support, memory for lyrics, volume control (loud AND soft on purpose), and the performance confidence that transfers to every show-and-tell after.

Words to learn

humechohighlowloudsoftchorussoloapplause

Say this to your child

“"Singing club is open! Warm up with me — hmmmm up high, hmmmm down low. Now echo this: la-la-LEAF! ... Your turn to lead. And now the big song — from the top!"”

Step by step

  1. Warm up the voice: hum the lowest note, glide to the highest, slide back down.
  2. Echo song: you sing a short line, the child echoes it — then swap leader roles.
  3. High-and-low game: sing the same word as a giant (low), a mouse (high), a sleepy bear (slow).
  4. Pick the song and sing it ALL the way through — mistakes are part of every concert.
  5. The performance: child takes the microphone, family is the audience, applause is mandatory, bow is optional but encouraged.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the singer holds the microphone slightly away and the other hand opens wide — singers use their whole body as the instrument’s sound box, which the wide hand is showing.

Ask your child

"Can your voice go higher? Lower?" "What does the echo do?" (copies the line) "Which part of the song is the chorus?" (the part everyone joins) "How does the audience say thank you?" (applause)

What your child can say or do

Your child may perform the song three times with costume changes, invent lyrics about the dog, or schedule a hallway concert — singers book their own tours.

Out in the real world

Singers, actors, teachers and broadcasters all train the speaking-singing voice. Every anthem, lullaby and happy-birthday is sung by people who hummed first.

Try it together

Add-a-word song: sing a familiar song but each player changes ONE word per line — the audience must catch every change. Singing, listening and laughing in one round.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do we warm up?" (hum up and down) "What does your voice do in the giant game?" (goes low) "Who leads the echo?" (whoever’s turn it is)

This lesson pairs with the Singing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Archery — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the archery club habit safely: real bows wait for the range and its trained coaches, while at home the aim, the breath and the stillness train first.

What is this?

Archery club is the target sport — draw, aim, hold, release — practiced under trained coaches at a proper range. The card’s printed skills are Aim & Focus: choosing the target and holding body and mind still until the moment. The home version trains everything EXCEPT the arrow.

What does it mean?

Archery is mostly a stillness sport: the shot happens in the pause, and the pause is trainable. Beanbag targets, sock throws and held poses all build the same two muscles — the eye that picks a target and the body that waits.

What does the child need to know?

At home: beanbags, a laundry basket or chalk target, clear space, and patience. At the range: a trained coach (certified), loaner bows sized for children, arm guards, and rules everyone follows before anything flies.

Why this matters

Aim-and-focus training transfers everywhere — throwing, catching, handwriting steadiness, and the emotional habit of one calm breath before any attempt. And the range visit, when it comes, lands on prepared ground: the child already knows how to aim and wait.

What it teaches

Target focus, breath control, stance stability, follow-through habits, and the safety mindset that real equipment deserves real training.

Words to learn

aimtargetfocusdrawholdreleaserangecoachbreath

Say this to your child

“"Archery club trains the aim first — the bows live at the range with the coaches. Home practice: beanbag, breath, freeze... and hold the pose! Focus is a muscle. Ready?"”

Step by step

  1. Home target one: beanbags at a hoop — three steps back, one slow breath, toss, and HOLD the follow-through pose for two seconds.
  2. Home target two: rolled socks at the laundry-basket bullseye — move back one step each round.
  3. The archer stance drill: feet apart, body tall, five-second freeze before every throw — the freeze is the actual archery.
  4. Breath habit: in through the nose, out slow, release ON the exhale — the same timing real archers use.
  5. When the family is ready: book a session at a proper range with a certified coach, and the child arrives already knowing how to aim, breathe and hold.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the archer’s arm guard sits snug against the sleeve and the bow is drawn halfway — real archery wears protection and starts with lessons, which is exactly why the coach comes before the arrows.

Ask your child

"When do we release in archery?" (on the slow exhale) "Why do we hold the pose after the throw?" (follow-through is aim’s last half) "Where do real bows live?" (the range, with trained coaches)

What your child can say or do

Your child may chalk bullseyes on every wall (outdoors, ideally), hold five-second freezes unprompted all week, or ask when the range visit happens — the answer: when the coach says yes.

Out in the real world

Olympic archers, bowhunters and historical reenactors all learned the same order: stance, breath, aim, then equipment. Coaches and ranges keep the sport safe — no exceptions, no shortcuts.

Try it together

Point-ladder tournament: each family member gets three beanbag throws from the same line, points by ring, and the ladder climbs one step back per round. Focus wins; laughter keeps the league alive.

Understanding check

Ask: "What trains before the bow?" (aim, breath, stance) "Who teaches real archery?" (a trained coach at a range) "What happens on the exhale?" (the release)

Staying safe

Ask a grown-up and a trained coach. Real bows and arrows belong at a proper range with certified instruction, safety gear and range rules — home practice trains aim and patience only, and never touches arrows.

This lesson pairs with the Archery flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Astronomy — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the astronomy club habit: a moon diary that fills in shape by shape, one bright planet found together, and the big-question hour where wonder does the teaching.

What is this?

Astronomy club is regular sky time — moon watching, star finding, question nights — where the printed skills are Wonder & Discovery: the big questions and the patient looking that answers them. It is the club that meets after bedtime and still gets permission.

What does it mean?

The moon diary teaches the deepest sky fact: the sky changes on schedule, and anyone can learn the schedule. Finding one planet teaches scale gently — that light traveled minutes or years to reach the eyes.

What does the child need to know?

A small notebook for the moon diary, a clear evening or two a week, a red flashlight (red keeps night eyes ready) if possible, and one star map or app. A window works; outdoors works better.

Why this matters

Astronomy builds observation over time, scale thinking and the honest habit of checking — is the moon really the same shape? It also seeds the physics questions every curious child eventually asks, with the sky already familiar ground.

What it teaches

Pattern observation across nights, recording discipline (dated drawings), scale and distance intuition, question-asking courage, and the patience of slow change.

Words to learn

moonphasecrescentplanetstartelescopeorbitskynight

Say this to your child

“"Astronomy club meets tonight! Bring the diary — first we guess tonight’s moon, then we look. Planets hold still, stars twinkle: which is that bright one? And every night ends with one question for next time."”

Step by step

  1. Start the moon diary: same notebook, same pencil, one dated drawing per clear night — shape and where it sat in the sky.
  2. Week two: the child predicts tonight’s moon shape BEFORE looking — astronomers guess, then check.
  3. Find one planet together: a steady bright light (planets hold still; stars twinkle) — Venus or Jupiter usually plays along.
  4. Star stories night: pick one constellation, learn its name and its story — the sky carried the library before books.
  5. The big-question hour: why does the moon change? what is a star? End every session with one question written down for next time — the club always leaves with homework from the sky.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the astronomer leans into a telescope on a tripod with one eye closed — the wink is half concentration and half delight, which is the honest face of discovery.

Ask your child

"What shape is tonight’s moon — and were we right?" "How do we tell a planet from a star?" (steady light vs twinkling) "What question did the sky give us tonight?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may guard the moon diary like a logbook, spot the moon in daylight (allowed — astronomers nod), or ask where the sun goes at night — which is the club’s favorite homework.

Out in the real world

Astronomers, satellite engineers and every navigation system in history run on sky patterns. The moon diary is a real observing log in miniature — dated drawings, honest checks.

Try it together

Backyard scale walk: if the sun were a soccer ball on the porch, the child walks the neighborhood model to find where Earth would sit — a marble about fifty meters away. Scale becomes walkable.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me a crescent with your hands." "Why do we date the diary?" (the sky changes on schedule) "What twinkles — planet or star?" (star)

This lesson pairs with the Astronomy flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Bird Watching — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the bird watching club habit: a tally sheet by the window, the three clues every bird gives away, and the naming ritual that turns visitors into regulars.

What is this?

Bird watching club is quiet observation time — window posts, park walks, and a notebook of who came. The card’s printed skills are Observe & Discover: watching closely and naming what appears. It is the quietest club in the school and one of the most addictive.

What does it mean?

Birds are identified by three clues — size, color, song — which trains structured observation: notice first, name second. The tally habit teaches counting with purpose and makes absence as interesting as presence (where did the big blue one go?).

What does the child need to know?

A window with a view of trees or feeders, a tally sheet, pencils, and quiet voices. Binoculars help but are optional at first; the feeder does the recruiting.

Why this matters

Bird watching builds patience, pattern memory and local ecology knowledge — the child learns which birds winter here, which pass through, and which bully the feeder. It is also the club most likely to produce a lifetime hobby.

What it teaches

Focused observation, listening discrimination (songs differ), data habits (tallies, dates), species vocabulary, and the stillness skill that helps in every quiet situation.

Words to learn

observebinocularsperchsongfeedertallyspecieshabitatflock

Say this to your child

“"Bird watching club, window post! Voices down, eyes up. Three clues: size, color, song... tally mark for the little brown one! Who is our most regular regular?"”

Step by step

  1. Post the tally sheet by the window with three bird columns to start.
  2. Learn the three clues together: how big (sparrow? pigeon?), what colors, what song.
  3. First observation window: five quiet minutes, tally marks for every visitor.
  4. Name the regulars: the three most common visitors get names in the notebook — real species names first, silly nicknames welcome as middle names.
  5. Weekly review: which bird leads the tally? which went missing? The notebook now tells a story about the yard itself.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the watcher holds binoculars ready but the eyes are on the bird directly — binoculars come after the naked-eye spotting, which is the club’s real order.

Ask your child

"Which three clues identify a bird?" (size, color, song) "Who leads our tally this week?" "Which bird has not come back?" "What could we put out for them?" (the feeder question — dangerous, wonderful)

What your child can say or do

Your child may learn songs faster than names, guard the tally sheet with a pencil on a string, or demand the feeder be filled at dawn — watchers become keepers.

Out in the real world

Ornithologists, park rangers and citizen-science counters all started with a window and a tally. The big bird counts every year run on exactly this notebook habit.

Try it together

Song match: play three bird songs, match each to the bird’s picture. Ears train slower than eyes — but once a song is learned, it is learned forever, and the yard turns audible.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the three bird clues." "What do we record on the tally sheet?" (every visit) "Why do we stay quiet?" (birds leave loud company)

This lesson pairs with the Bird Watching flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Calligraphy — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the calligraphy club habit: one letter per session, ten honest attempts, and the artist’s signature that turns practice into a print.

What is this?

Calligraphy club is slow, deliberate lettering — a pen or even a pencil held right, strokes drawn rather than written. The card’s printed skills are Letters & Patience: beautiful forms and the calm they ask for.

What does it mean?

Calligraphy teaches that a letter is a shape with rules: downstrokes thick, upstrokes thin, the pen moving at walking speed. Practicing ONE letter ten ways trains deep focus better than writing ten letters once.

What does the child need to know?

A soft pencil, marker or beginner calligraphy pen, smooth paper, and a comfortable chair. Ruled guide lines drawn in pencil help every attempt stay honest.

Why this matters

Calligraphy builds fine-motor control, stroke awareness (the same thick-thin logic lives in every handwritten alphabet) and genuine patience — the club where rushing shows instantly, and slowing down pays visibly.

What it teaches

Pen grip and pressure control, stroke consistency, letterform eyes (spotting what differs from the model), focus stamina, and the finishing habit of signing work.

Words to learn

strokedownstrokeupstrokethickthinscriptflourishsign

Say this to your child

“"Calligraphy club! Slow pens write prettiest — downstrokes THICK, upstrokes thin, arm moving like a slow train. One letter today, ten tries. Which one is your best?"”

Step by step

  1. Grip check: relaxed hand, pen low, whole arm moving — not just fingers.
  2. Practice strokes before letters: rows of thick bars down, thin lines up.
  3. Pick ONE letter and draw it huge, then medium, then tiny — a family of the same letter.
  4. The ten-attempt page: one letter, ten tries, each honest — circle the best one.
  5. Sign the page like an artist signs a print, date it, and the best letter earns the fridge (or a frame if the family is smart).

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the letter A on the page flows with a curved entry stroke and an ink pot waits beside the pen — calligraphy letters begin with a move, the way dancers enter a step.

Ask your child

"Which strokes are thick — up or down?" (down) "Why do we practice one letter ten times?" (depth beats speed) "What does an artist do at the bottom of the page?" (signs it)

What your child can say or do

Your child may flourish every letter with unnecessary swirls (encouraged), write the family’s names in script for gifts, or slow down noticeably on school writing — habits migrate.

Out in the real world

Wedding invitations, logos, movie titles and city signs all use lettering someone drew. Calligraphers still earn real money for exactly what the club practiced today.

Try it together

Name gallery: each family member’s name gets written in the child’s best lettering and framed on one wall — the house’s permanent exhibition, updated as the skill grows.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me the pen speed." (slow) "Which stroke is thick?" (the downstroke) "How many tries does practice get?" (ten — then we circle the best)

This lesson pairs with the Calligraphy flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Chess — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the chess club habit: learn the pieces in value order, play pawn chess before full chess, and install the club’s one law — think first, touch second.

What is this?

Chess club is regular board time — piece moves, simple openings, honest games — where the printed skills are Focus & Strategy: holding the board in the head and planning two moves ahead.

What does it mean?

Chess teaches consequence: every move answers a question (what does this allow?). Starting with pawns-only games lets the child feel the board before the full army arrives. Losing small games early is the training; the handshake is the graduation.

What does the child need to know?

A chess set (any set — paper cutouts work), a table with no TV in sight, and ten unhurried minutes per game. A notebook for favorite positions is optional and obsessive in the best way.

Why this matters

Chess builds planning, pattern memory and losing-gracefully — three skills every classroom wants. It is also the club that most reliably upgrades family game night.

What it teaches

Move-by-move planning, piece-value intuition, rule memory, losing without collapsing, winning without gloating, and focus stretches that grow with every game.

Words to learn

piecepawnknightrookcheckcheckmatemoveboardstrategy

Say this to your child

“"Chess club! Meet the smallest soldier: the pawn walks forward but captures sideways. Pawn game first — first pawn to the other side wins. And the law of the club: think, THEN touch."”

Step by step

  1. Meet the army in value order: pawn (the small worker), knight (the jumper), bishop, rook, queen, king — one move demo each.
  2. Play pawn chess first: pawns only, first to reach the far side wins — three fast games.
  3. Add one piece at a time across future sessions — knights next (they jump, which delights everyone).
  4. Install the law: think, THEN touch — a touched piece is a moved piece, gently enforced.
  5. End with the handshake ritual: every game, win or lose — the habit outlasts every opening.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the player’s fingers hover just above a black piece without touching it — the card froze the exact moment before the move, which is where chess actually lives.

Ask your child

"Which piece jumps over others?" (the knight) "What is the club’s law?" (think, then touch) "What do we say at the end of every game?" (good game — handshake)

What your child can say or do

Your child may develop a favorite piece (knights win most hearts), set up famous checkmates for the family, or narrate the board like a sports commentator — chess clubs produce personalities.

Out in the real world

Grandmasters, programmers and strategists all trained on this board. Schools teach chess because planning two moves ahead is half of every school subject.

Try it together

Knight’s tour mini: place one knight on the board and try to land on every square color in a row of eight jumps — the jumping pattern learns itself through play.

Understanding check

Ask: "How does the pawn capture?" (diagonally) "What do we do before touching a piece?" (think) "Show me where the king starts."

This lesson pairs with the Chess flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Choir — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the choir club habit: breathe together first, sing rounds second, and end with a two-part song where the family genuinely becomes a choir.

What is this?

Choir club is group singing with listening at the center — unison songs, rounds, and simple two-part harmonies. The card’s printed skills are Voice & Harmony: your own sound and the art of fitting it to everyone else’s.

What does it mean?

Singing in a group trains the ear more than the throat: holding your part while another part moves is advanced listening. Rounds (the same song, started at different times) teach harmony without needing to teach harmony.

What does the child need to know?

A song everyone knows by heart, a room where voices can be loud, and hands for conducting waves. Assign parts only after the unison feels solid.

Why this matters

Choir builds breath control, pitch matching and the social skill of blending — being heard AND hearing. Group singing also synchronizes breathing and heartbeats, which is the science behind why choirs feel so good.

What it teaches

Pitch accuracy, breath management, part independence (holding one line among many), ensemble listening, and performance courage shared across the group.

Words to learn

unisonroundpartharmonyblendchorusbreathconductorensemble

Say this to your child

“"Choir club, everyone in! Breathe with me — four in, four out, hisssss. Now all together... and now the MAGIC: you start, and when you reach the mountain, WE start the song over. Listen to us weave!"”

Step by step

  1. Breathing first: four counts in through the nose, four out with a hiss — three rounds, everyone together.
  2. Unison song: the whole family sings one familiar song straight through.
  3. The round: half the family starts, the other half joins two lines later — Row Your Boat is the classic; the weaving is the wow.
  4. Two-part play: half sings a steady oooh drone, half sings the melody above it — swap roles and listen to both.
  5. The concert: one song, both parts, one bow — family choirs deserve audiences and audiences deserve family choirs.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the singer holds the songbook open at singing distance and the mouth is mid-vowel — choirs read and listen simultaneously, which is why the book sits low and the ears stay in charge.

Ask your child

"What did the round sound like?" (the same song chasing itself) "What was your job in the drone part?" (steady and soft) "What makes a choir different from solo singing?" (listening while singing)

What your child can say or do

Your child may conduct the family with full authority, assign the pet a part, or start rounds at dinner without warning — choirs infiltrate households.

Out in the real world

Choirs, a cappella groups, gospel ensembles and every national anthem sung in a stadium run on this training. Professional singers still warm up with the same hiss-breath.

Try it together

Conductor game: one player waves big hands (louder), small hands (softer), a fist (stop) while the choir sings — the conductor swaps every verse, and control of volume becomes a game.

Understanding check

Ask: "What comes first, breathing or singing?" (breathing) "What is a round?" (the same song started late) "What do we do while another part sings?" (listen and hold our line)

This lesson pairs with the Choir flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Climbing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the climbing club habit safely: walls, ropes and harnesses live at the gym with trained staff, while at home the grips, balance and climbing logic train first.

What is this?

Climbing club is movement up walls — holds, routes, harnesses and ropes — practiced where trained belayers work. The card’s printed skills are Courage & Movement: the nerve to move up and the body control to do it well. The home version trains grip, balance and route-thinking.

What does it mean?

Climbing teaches route-reading: look up, plan the hand order, then move. The three-point rule (always two hands and a foot, or two feet and a hand, in contact) is the secret geometry of every climb — trainable on stairs, curbs and playground frames.

What does the child need to know?

At home: a playground bar, a curb, stairs, and patience. At the gym: a certified wall, fitted harness, trained belayer, and the child’s own two planning eyes. Nothing climbs without the rope team.

Why this matters

Climbing builds grip and upper-body strength, planning under excitement, and the specific confidence of doing something that looked impossible from the ground. It is also a thinking sport wearing an adventure costume.

What it teaches

Grip strength, route planning, three-point-contact habits, balance under height (perceived), and the courage loop: look, plan, move, rest, repeat.

Words to learn

holdgriprouteharnessbelaywallreachrestclimb

Say this to your child

“"Climbing club trains the body first — the walls live at the gym with the rope team. Curb walk... bar hang, two more seconds... and up the stairs with three points always holding. What’s our next route?"”

Step by step

  1. Home drill one — the curb walk: heel-to-toe along a curb, arms out, no falls allowed on the ground next to it (which makes it feel official).
  2. Home drill two — bar hang: hold the playground bar two seconds longer than last time, counted out loud.
  3. Home drill three — three-point stairs: climb slowly touching only after two other points are placed; narrate hand-hand-foot-foot.
  4. Route games: pick a sequence up the playground ladder — left hand high rung, right hand low, feet follow — planned BEFORE moving.
  5. When the family is ready: the gym visit, where harness, rope and trained belayer are standard — the child arrives already reading routes and holding grips.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the climber wears the helmet snug and grips the rope with a hand wrapped fully around — real climbing is dressed for it, which is why the gear comes before the glory.

Ask your child

"What is the three-point rule?" (two hands and a foot, or two feet and a hand) "What do we plan before we climb?" (the route) "Who holds the rope at the gym?" (the trained belayer)

What your child can say or do

Your child may three-point every staircase in the house, time bar hangs with a stopwatch, or narrate the climbing wall like a mountain expedition — grip strength arrives before confidence; confidence follows.

Out in the real world

Rock climbers, arborists, rescue teams and stunt performers all train route-reading and grip first. The gym wall is the safest classroom in adventure sports.

Try it together

Floor-is-lava route planning: mark five safe spots across the living room, plan the crossing order out loud, then cross with three-point rules on the armrests. Planning first, moving second — always.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me the three-point rule on the stairs." "What comes first — move or plan?" (plan) "How long can you hang?" (two seconds more than last week)

This lesson pairs with the Climbing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Coding — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the coding club habit: instructions given exactly, errors welcomed as information, and the discovery that a computer (or a parent) does what you SAID, not what you MEANT.

What is this?

Coding club is instruction-writing time — real block programming on screen, or the offline version where family members run the program. The card’s printed skills are Logic & Discovery: ordered steps and the joy of finding what works.

What does it mean?

Coding is sequencing made visible: step one, step two, a loop when something repeats, and a bug whenever the meaning got lost between the idea and the instruction. Debugging teaches the healthiest error attitude in education — mistakes are data.

What does the child need to know?

Offline: paper strips for steps, a willing robot (any family member), and small obstacles. On screen: any beginner block-coding app — the club starts with moves and loops, not typing.

Why this matters
