Coding builds sequencing, prediction and systematic troubleshooting — and it reframes mistakes as the fastest way to learn. The skills transfer to math word problems, science procedure and every recipe in the house.

What it teaches

Sequencing and ordering, precise vocabulary (forward, turn, repeat), prediction (what will the program do?), debugging patience, and the pride of a program that runs.

Words to learn

codeprogramstepsequenceloopbugdebugruncommand

Say this to your child

“"Coding club! I am the robot — give me exact steps for a sandwich. Take bread... wait, you never said open the bag! Robots follow instructions EXACTLY. Let’s debug our program."”

Step by step

  1. Robot-parent warm-up: the child programs you to make a sandwich — obey every instruction LITERALLY (circle means spin, missing steps mean chaos).
  2. Debrief: which step was missing? which word was unclear? Rewrite and re-run until the sandwich happens.
  3. Sequence cards: five picture steps shuffled; the child orders them, then the program runs as ordered — success or funny failure, either is information.
  4. Introduce the loop: clapping three times becomes clap... REPEAT 3 — the moment programming gets powerful.
  5. On screen: one block program — move, turn, move, REPEAT — running a character to a goal, then one deliberate bug to debug together.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the programmer’s hands rest on the laptop mid-thought, eyes already half-smiling — the card caught the moment BEFORE the run, which is where every program is still perfect.

Ask your child

"What does the robot do with unclear steps?" (its own silly version) "What is a bug?" (an instruction that fooled us) "What fixed it?" (debugging — reading, guessing, testing) "Where else do we use step-by-step plans?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may program the walk to school in forty steps, write a loop for bedtime complaints (suspicious), or demand the robot game nightly — precision players do.

Out in the real world

Every app, game, dishwasher cycle and traffic light runs on written instructions. Programmers are the people who write them and then debug what they meant.

Try it together

Treasure-program: hide a toy, write the six-step program to reach it on cards, run the program as written — then debug together where it went sideways. The bug is always the best part.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does a computer do with instructions?" (exactly what was written) "What do we call finding a mistake?" (debugging) "Show me a loop with your hands." (clap, repeat, repeat)

This lesson pairs with the Coding flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Cycling — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the cycling club habit: the helmet rule that never bends, the balance-first method that skips training wheels, and the celebration protocol for the first glide.

What is this?

Cycling club is bike time with a sequence — balance before pedals, brakes before speed, adventure after control. The card’s printed skills are Balance & Adventure: staying upright and going somewhere new on your own power.

What does it mean?

The balance-first method works because pedaling is the EASY part: gliding with feet up teaches the body what balance feels like, and the pedals reattach as a promotion. Braking practice comes before speed — stopping is the skill that earns the adventure.

What does the child need to know?

A bike sized so both feet reach the ground flat, a helmet that fits level (two-finger rule at the brow), an open flat surface, and patience. Optional: a spanner to take the pedals off for the gliding phase.

Why this matters

Cycling builds balance, leg strength and real independence — the first vehicle a child drives alone. The learning sequence also teaches practice culture: small stages, each one celebrated, none skipped.

What it teaches

Dynamic balance, braking judgment, steering-while-looking (eyes go where the bike goes), stamina, and the road-safety habits that come with the freedom.

Words to learn

helmetbalanceglidepedalbrakesteerrideblockadventure

Say this to your child

“"Cycling club! Helmet check — level, two fingers, snug. Now scoot... scoot... FEET UP — glide! Count it: one, two, three, FOUR seconds of flying. The pedals are waiting for your promotion."”

Step by step

  1. Helmet ceremony: level on the head, two fingers at the brow, strap snug — the helmet rides every ride, no exceptions, and the child states the rule back.
  2. Scoot phase: pedals off, push with both feet, then LONG glides with feet up — count the seconds of each glide.
  3. Brake rehearsal: walk the bike squeezing both brakes gently — feel the stop before needing it.
  4. Pedals return: one foot up, one push, eyes FORWARD not down — glides become rides within a session or two.
  5. The first route: the block, the grown-up beside, the child steering — celebrate at the door with the full podium ceremony the family has prepared.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the helmet sits properly strapped and the rider stands OVER the bike rather than on it — real cyclists dress first and mount second, which is the club’s entire safety culture in one image.

Ask your child

"What is the two-finger rule?" (helmet fit at the brow) "What do we learn BEFORE pedals?" (gliding balance) "Where do our eyes go when steering?" (forward — the bike follows) "What do we squeeze to stop?" (both brakes, gently)

What your child can say or do

Your child may count glides like flight records, brake-test on every driveway, or plan the block route with a drawn map — cyclists are route people from day one.

Out in the real world

Couriers, racers, bike mechanics and every kid with a paper route run on this skill. The glide-to-pedal method is how most modern riding schools teach — training wheels skipped entirely.

Try it together

Glide olympics: three events — longest glide (feet up), straightest line between two chalk marks, smoothest stop at the line. Medals are mandatory; podium photos eternal.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me the helmet check." "What do we practice with feet up?" (gliding) "When do the pedals come back?" (after the glides are long) "What do we squeeze to stop?"

This lesson pairs with the Cycling flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Debate — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the debate club habit: silly questions first, structured arguing second, and the switch-sides round that trains empathy as a formal event.

What is this?

Debate club is structured disagreement — a question, two sides, reasons and listening. The card’s printed skills are Speak & Listen: making a point clearly and hearing the other one properly.

What does it mean?

Debate separates opinion (I like winter) from argument (winter builds snow forts, which...). The format trains three things at once: organized speaking, active listening, and the humility experiment of arguing the side you did not pick.

What does the child need to know?

A question worth two opinions (pancakes or waffles? cats or dogs?), a timer, two chairs facing, and the family rulebook: one voice at a time, every reason gets heard, hands stay calm.

Why this matters

Debate builds sentence-level confidence, reason-giving, note-listening and emotional control under disagreement — the exact skills classrooms and democracies run on. Silly topics keep it safe while the machinery gets strong.

What it teaches

Organized speaking (first, second, finally), listening with memory (repeating the other side’s best point), persuasion vocabulary, turn discipline, and empathy by assignment.

Words to learn

debatesidereasonpointrespondlistenfairagreepersuade

Say this to your child

“"Debate night! Tonight’s question: are cats or dogs the better pet? Pick your side, gather two reasons... and remember the rule: before you answer, you repeat their best point. Speak AND listen."”

Step by step

  1. Announce tonight’s question and let each speaker pick a side — coin flip if both want the same one.
  2. Two minutes of silent reason-gathering: each speaker writes or thinks of TWO reasons.
  3. Opening statements: side A, then side B — one voice, other ears listening.
  4. The response round: each side repeats the OTHER side’s best reason before answering it — the listening guarantee.
  5. Switch sides and argue the opposite view for two minutes, then vote by applause — and name the best reason anyone said, regardless of side.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the speaker’s finger is up but the microphone is close — the raised finger means I have the floor, and the microphone means the room has agreed to listen. Both halves make a debate.

Ask your child

"What was their best reason?" (prove it was heard) "What is YOUR second reason?" "How did it feel to argue the other side?" "What should next week’s question be?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may argue breakfast choices with formal openings, referee sibling disputes using the repeat-their-point rule, or request debate night as a weekly fixture — the club scales.

Out in the real world

Lawyers, journalists, scientists and every good meeting run on reason-listen-respond. The switch-sides trick is used in real mediation training — families just run it with waffles.

Try it together

Question hat: twenty silly questions on paper, one drawn per night, sides assigned by coin flip. By round ten, the family argues in complete sentences at high speed — a parenting miracle.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the one-voice rule?" (speakers take turns, listeners listen) "What must you do before answering?" (repeat their best reason) "Why do we switch sides?" (to understand the other view)

This lesson pairs with the Debate flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Fencing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the fencing club habit safely: blades and masks live at the club with trained coaches, while at home the footwork, lunge and salute train on carpet with zero equipment.

What is this?

Fencing club is swordplay with a rulebook — footwork, blade work, bouts under supervision. The card’s printed skills are Agility & Focus: fast, light feet and total attention on one opponent. The home version trains everything below the shoulder.

What does it mean?

Fencing is chess at running speed: distance, timing and the habit of reacting to what the opponent offers, not what you hoped. The salute comes first because the sport formalized politeness into its reflexes — respect is muscle memory here.

What does the child need to know?

At home: smooth floor space, a pillow for the head-posture drill, and socks. At the club: mask, jacket, glove, blade — all fitted and checked by a trained coach, with bouts supervised at all times.

Why this matters

Fencing builds leg strength, reaction speed and one-on-one focus like nothing else — and the discipline culture transfers: salute, line up, thank the referee. Kids who fence learn to lose fast and reset faster.

What it teaches

Footwork speed (advance, retreat), lunge mechanics, distance judgment, reaction focus, and the etiquette reflexes that make the sport safe.

Words to learn

saluteadvanceretreatlungeboutmaskbladecoachtouch

Say this to your child

“"Fencing club! Salute first — arm out, small bow. Now on guard: knees soft, feet apart. Advance... retreat... and the pillow rides on your head! Five slow lunges — the coach will love these feet."”

Step by step

  1. The salute first — arm extended, bow of the head: practice it with full ceremony; it is the sport’s signature.
  2. Footwork drill: on-guard stance (knees soft, feet apart), then five advances, five retreats, smooth as a dance step.
  3. Pillow posture: balance a pillow on the head during the footwork — the drill that keeps chins up and shoulders level.
  4. The lunge: back foot planted, front foot slides, front knee bends over the toe — five slow lunges, five quick, pillow staying put.
  5. When the family is ready: the club visit, where mask, jacket and coach are standard — the child arrives with footwork the coach can build on.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the sword points DOWN while the mask waits in the other hand — the card shows the sport’s manners: blade lowered, salute first, mask on before anything else happens.

Ask your child

"What comes before every bout?" (the salute) "Name the three footwork moves." (advance, retreat, lunge) "Why does the pillow ride on the head?" (posture — chin up, shoulders level) "Where do the blades live?" (the club, with the coach)

What your child can say or do

Your child may salute before entering rooms, lunge across the hallway at napkins, or march pillow-drills nightly — the coach will confirm the feet are ready before any blade is.

Out in the real world

Olympic fencers, stage combat performers and historians of the duel all trained footwork first. Clubs worldwide accept students on exactly this plan: feet ready, then equipment.

Try it together

Mirror footwork: one player leads (advance, retreat, lunge), the other mirrors in real time — leader swaps every ten moves. Reaction speed grows without a single blade.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me the salute." "Demonstrate the lunge slowly." "What does the coach provide at the club?" (masks, jackets, blades — and supervision)

Staying safe

Ask a grown-up and a trained coach. Blades, masks and jackets are fitted and checked by experts, and every bout happens under a coach’s eye — home practice is footwork and posture only, never with a blade.

This lesson pairs with the Fencing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Fashion Design — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the fashion design club habit: design briefs before drawings, collections before single outfits, and the runway show that makes every designer present their thinking.

What is this?

Fashion design club is designing clothes on paper first, in fabric when ready — sketches, swatches, paper dolls and one showstopper idea. The card’s printed skills are Imagine & Create: inventing the garment and building it with the hands.

What does it mean?

Design starts with a brief (who wears this? for what weather? doing what?) because clothes are problem-solving — raincoats solve rain. Sketching three options before choosing trains the designer’s core habit: ideas improve in plural.

What does the child need to know?

Paper and pencils, a paper-doll template, fabric scraps or old clothes for swatches, tape, and safety scissors. A grown-up owns any real needle-and-thread work; the designer owns the ideas.

Why this matters

Fashion design builds drawing, planning and material thinking — plus the presentation skills of explaining a collection. It is art class and engineering class sharing a sketchbook.

What it teaches

Design thinking (brief, options, choice), drawing with intent, fabric-texture awareness, fine-motor pinning and taping, and the presenting confidence of the runway.

Words to learn

designsketchfabricswatchcollectionbriefrunwayalterstitch

Say this to your child

“"Fashion design club! Tonight’s brief: SNOW EXPEDITION — who is it for, and what must the outfit survive? Three sketches, then pick your winner and tell us why. The runway opens at eight!"”

Step by step

  1. The brief first: draw a card — RAINY DAY, BIRTHDAY PARTY, SNOW EXPEDITION — and read it out loud.
  2. Three sketches minimum: the same brief, three different outfits — big shapes first, details after.
  3. Choose the winner and defend it: why does this one solve the brief best? Designers present, they do not just draw.
  4. Fabric board: pick real scraps or cut paper swatches for the winning outfit — texture labels (soft, stiff, shiny) written beside each.
  5. The runway show: paper dolls model the collection on the hallway runway, the designer narrates each look, and the audience asks the brief questions back.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the designer holds real pink fabric in one hand and a finished dress sketch in the other — the two hands show the club’s whole pipeline: fabric goes in, idea comes out, then back to fabric.

Ask your child

"What does the brief ask the outfit to DO?" "Why did you pick this sketch over the others?" "What is this fabric’s personality?" (soft? stiff? loud?) "What is next season’s brief?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may brief the family’s real closets, sketch a collection for the cat (market exists), or label swatches with fabric names learned from labels — designers research.

Out in the real world

Fashion designers, costume departments, pattern makers and merchandisers all run on brief-sketch-fabric. The runway show is a real industry ritual the family can host tonight.

Try it together

Alter challenge: one old T-shirt per player and tape only — restyle it into something new for the paper doll, then present the alteration story: what it was, what it became.

Understanding check

Ask: "What comes first — sketch or brief?" (brief) "How many sketches before choosing?" (three) "What does the designer do at the runway?" (narrates the collection)

This lesson pairs with the Fashion Design flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Filmmaking — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the filmmaking club habit: plan in three scenes, shoot with steady hands, and end every film with a premiere — lights down, popcorn optional, credits mandatory.

What is this?

Filmmaking club is story time with a camera — planning shots, filming takes, editing by simply choosing the best take. The card’s printed skills are Imagine & Tell: inventing the scenes and getting them on screen.

What does it mean?

Film forces planning: a three-scene structure (beginning, middle, end) fits in one sentence, which teaches story economy. Interviews teach question-asking; bloopers teach editing judgment — what stays, what goes.

What does the child need to know?

Any phone or tablet camera, a stable surface or improvised tripod (bookstack, cup), one story idea, and actors from the family. Ten minutes of footage maximum — shorts are honest.

Why this matters

Filmmaking builds narrative planning, technical patience (steady shots, retakes) and editing judgment. It also teaches the deepest media-literacy lesson early: every video someone watches was CHOSEN this way.

What it teaches

Story structure, shot planning, steady-hand technique, interview questions, directing language (action, cut, again), and the finishing discipline of a premiere.

Words to learn

sceneshottakeactioncutinterviewcreditspremieredirector

Say this to your child

“"Filmmaking club! Three scenes, one sentence each — starting, trouble, ending. Steady hands... lights... and ACTION! Cut! That was take one — do we keep it or shoot again?"”

Step by step

  1. The three-scene plan: one sentence per scene — how it starts, what goes wrong, how it ends. Written down, always.
  2. Steady-shot school: elbows in, camera held with two hands or propped — film ten seconds of nothing until the hands learn stillness.
  3. Scene by scene: film each planned scene twice — take one and take two — then watch both immediately and CHOOSE.
  4. The interview scene: one reporter, five prepared questions, one subject in character — the easiest scene and the funniest.
  5. The premiere: couch, lights low, film plays, everyone claps, credits roll (everyone’s name, including the camera).

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the camera operator holds the camera at eye level with both hands wrapped firm — the card demonstrates the club’s first skill: steady hands before fancy moves.

Ask your child

"What are our three scenes?" "Why did we keep take two?" (watch both and decide — editing is choosing) "Whose name goes in the credits?" (everybody — including the camera)

What your child can say or do

Your child may film the dog’s day in five acts, direct parents with startling authority, or insist on retakes until the delivery is perfect — directors are born in living rooms.

Out in the real world

YouTubers, animators, news crews and advertisers all work in three-scene thinking. Every movie credit lists a job the child held today — director included.

Try it together

Bloopers reel: save the funniest failed takes and end every premiere with them — the tradition teaches that mistakes are material, and the audience genuinely loves them most.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name our three scenes." "How do we hold the camera?" (steady, two hands, elbows in) "What plays after the film?" (the credits — everyone’s name)

This lesson pairs with the Filmmaking flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

First Aid — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the first aid club habit: rehearse the drill on stuffed patients, learn the real emergency number out loud, and train the calm voice that helps most.

What is this?

First aid club is helping-skills practice — scrapes, bruises, scared siblings and the drill of who to call. The card’s printed skills are Help & Care: knowing the steps and staying kind while doing them.

What does it mean?

First aid works because it is rehearsed: a rehearsed helper checks the scene, calls the grown-up or emergency number, and stays with the hurt person. Practicing on stuffed animals builds the sequence into reflex — and the calm voice into habit.

What does the child need to know?

A play first-aid kit (or real bandages), stuffed patients, the family’s real emergency number written large, and a grown-up co-teaching. Small scrapes are practice-able; everything bigger belongs to grown-ups and professionals.

Why this matters

Children who rehearse emergencies act instead of freezing — the checked-and-called sequence saves time in real events. The club also builds the helper identity: this child is useful in a crisis, which changes how the whole family feels.

What it teaches

Sequence memory (check, call, care), emergency number recall, calm-voice practice, gentle hands for bandaging, and the judgment to know when help is bigger than you.

Words to learn

first aidcheckcallcalmbandagescrapeemergencyhelpbrave

Say this to your child

“"First aid club! Our patient has a scrape. Check first — what happened? Small? Then we care: clean cloth, gentle wrap. And the number — say it with me: [emergency number]. Again. Again."”

Step by step

  1. The drill with a stuffed patient: check — what happened? is it small (scrape) or big (call the grown-up NOW)?
  2. Call practice: the emergency number recited out loud three times, then the address — number and address are the club’s spelling test.
  3. Care with calm words: rehearse the helper script — you are okay, I am here, help is coming — in the calmest voice available.
  4. Bandage school: clean cloth, wrap snug not tight, tape the end — practice on the teddy’s paw until smooth.
  5. The graduation scenario: one full drill, start to finish, child leading, grown-up observing — the certificate is a real bandage kept in the child’s own kit.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the red kit is closed with the white cross facing out and the helper’s hand is steady — the kit matters less than the trained hand, which is the card’s whole message.

Ask your child

"What are the three steps?" (check, call, care) "What is our emergency number?" (recite it) "What do we say to a scared patient?" (you are okay, I am here) "When do we call a grown-up instead of fixing it ourselves?" (always for big things)

What your child can say or do

Your child may bandage every stuffed animal in the house, recite the number at dinner unprompted, or coach a sibling through a real scrape with startling calm — helpers emerge fast.

Out in the real world

Nurses, lifeguards, camp counselors and search-and-rescue volunteers all run on rehearsed basics. Real first-aid courses teach children the same check-call-care from age eight upward.

Try it together

Emergency number song: sing the digits to a familiar tune three times a week until the number is permanently installed — then the address in the same melody.

Understanding check

Ask: "Recite the three steps." "Say the emergency number." "Show the calm-voice script." "Where does the bandage go on teddy?" (snug, not tight)

This lesson pairs with the First Aid flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Gymnastics — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the gymnastics club habit: warm up like animals, roll safely on soft ground, hold real balances, and stretch at the end like it matters — because it does.

What is this?

Gymnastics club is body-control training — rolls, balances, bridges and stretches on mats or soft ground. The card’s printed skills are Strength & Flexibility: power and range trained as one pair.

What does it mean?

Gymnastics teaches control before tricks: the safe roll (chin tucked, soft ground) comes before any flip, and the fall is rehearsed on purpose so surprises stay safe. Balance holds train the small muscles that running and writing both borrow.

What does the child need to know?

A mattress, rug or grass patch, loose clothes, and clear space. Barefoot grips better than socks. A grown-up spotter stands near for anything that leaves the ground.

Why this matters

Gymnastics builds strength, flexibility, spatial awareness and the fear-management habit — trying the thing after rehearsing the safety. It feeds every other sport quietly from underneath.

What it teaches

Core strength, flexibility (measured by the stretching ladder), rolling technique, balance endurance, and the courage loop: rehearse, attempt, celebrate, repeat.

Words to learn

rolltuckbalancebridgestretchspottermatholdflexible

Say this to your child

“"Gymnastics club! Animals first — bear, crab, frog... warm. Now tuck that chin — round back, roll! ... Now hold the flamingo. Count with me: one, two, three, FOUR seconds of statue."”

Step by step

  1. Animal warm-up: bear walk, crab walk, frog jumps, lizard crawl — two minutes, breathing hard.
  2. The safe roll: on soft ground, chin tucked to chest, hands flat, roll over the rounded back — three slow rolls, spotter beside.
  3. Balance holds: flamingo (one foot, arms out), then the scale (one leg back, arms forward) — count the seconds aloud.
  4. The bridge attempt (only when warm): hands and feet down, belly to the sky — even a small lift counts and gets celebrated.
  5. The stretching ladder: reach for toes (knees can bend), hold ten; butterfly stretch; the slow count to twenty while the muscles lengthen — flexibility is the club’s quietest skill and its most lasting.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the gymnast’s split is low to the floor with the arm waving high — the card shows the two skills as one picture: strength holds the body up, flexibility lets it open.

Ask your child

"What do we tuck before rolling?" (the chin) "Why do we practice on mats?" (soft landings make brave bodies) "Show me your longest balance hold." "What stretches longer every week?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may roll across every mattress in the house, practice bridges during TV time, or chart flexibility progress on the fridge — gymnasts track everything.

Out in the real world

Gymnasts, divers, dancers and martial artists all train rolls, balances and bridges. Physical therapists teach the same safe-roll to grandparents — it is a lifelong skill.

Try it together

Balance tag: everyone balances on one foot; the tagger moves slowly and tags anyone who puts the foot down — laughter guaranteed, balance trained under pressure.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me the animal warm-up." "What do we tuck in a roll?" (chin) "Name two balance poses." (flamingo, scale) "What does the spotter do?" (stays close for safety)

This lesson pairs with the Gymnastics flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Horse Riding — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the horse riding club habit safely: the greeting and grooming come before any riding, the instructor owns the mounted lessons, and the posture trains at home on a chair.

What is this?

Horse riding club is time with horses — greeting, grooming, walking and (with instructors) riding. The card’s printed skills are Courage & Care: steady nerve around something huge and gentle, and the grooming that earns trust.

What does it mean?

Horses read bodies: a calm rider gets a calm horse, which makes emotional regulation the sport’s first skill. Grooming before riding teaches the order real equestrians keep — care comes first, always.

What does the child need to know?

At the stable: an instructor, a helmet that fits, and a school horse that has met a thousand beginners. At home: a chair for posture drills, a soft brush for practicing strokes on a willing dog, and a calm voice.

Why this matters

Riding builds confidence, empathy and body awareness — and the responsibility of caring for a large animal is unlike anything else in childhood. Stable lessons also teach the courage math: being scared and doing it slowly anyway.

What it teaches

Emotional regulation, gentle-hand skills, posture muscles, pattern memory (greeting ritual), and the patience of working with a partner who cannot be hurried.

Words to learn

groommountreintrotstableinstructorhelmetcalmtrust

Say this to your child

“"Horse riding club starts on the ground — we greet first: come from the side, speak softly, flat hand out. Now grooming, long slow strokes... the horse tells us with its ears how we are doing."”

Step by step

  1. The greeting ritual: approach from the side, speak first (so the horse knows you are there), offer a flat hand to sniff — rehearse the script at home.
  2. Grooming: soft brush, long strokes along the hair growth, the horse’s favorite spots learned by watching its ears — care before riding, every single time.
  3. Home posture drill: chair-mount practice — sit tall, pretend reins held soft, eyes up, shoulders back — five slow minutes.
  4. Voice practice: horses respond to tone — rehearse the steady whoa and the encouraging cluck at a calm volume.
  5. The stable visit, when ready: instructor-led mounting, walking on a lead rein — everything above was the preparation, the ride is the celebration.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the helmet is on and the arms wrap the horse’s neck in a hug — the card shows the club’s truth: the relationship is the sport, and the hug is earned in grooming minutes.

Ask your child

"How do we greet a horse?" (side approach, speak first, flat hand) "What comes before riding?" (grooming) "Show me the riding posture on the chair." "Why do we use a calm voice?" (horses read tone)

What your child can say or do

Your child may practice the greeting on every large dog, groom the cat for tolerance points, or sit chair-mounted through dinner (posture is posture) — riders count days to the stable.

Out in the real world

Riding instructors, equestrian therapists, jockeys and ranchers all learned the ground skills first. Every riding school on Earth teaches grooming before mounting — no exceptions.

Try it together

Stable manager game: draw the day’s care chart for a pretend horse — breakfast, groom, exercise, water, bedtime check — and run the schedule with a stuffed horse all afternoon. Care becomes a routine with a name.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me the flat-hand greeting." "What do we always wear at the stable?" (the helmet) "What comes first, riding or grooming?" (grooming — every time) "What does a calm voice tell the horse?" (you are safe with me)

This lesson pairs with the Horse Riding flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Journaling — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the journaling club habit: a notebook that belongs to the child completely, three lines a day, and the rules that make it survive — no spelling tests, no reading aloud, no missing the honest bits.

What is this?

Journaling club is daily notebook time — three lines about today, or a drawing, or a list, in a book nobody checks. The card’s printed skills are Reflect & Express: looking back at the day and getting it onto paper.

What does it mean?

Journaling converts days into sentences, which is reflection in its smallest workable unit. The privacy rule is the engine: a journal nobody reads becomes honest, and honest writing is where the thinking actually happens.

What does the child need to know?

One notebook (chosen by the writer — the cover matters), one pencil that lives with it, and two minutes at the same time daily — bedtime and after school both work. Nothing else.

Why this matters

Journaling builds emotional vocabulary, memory for one’s own life, sentence confidence and the rarest skill in childhood: sitting with a thought long enough to write it. Rereading old entries later is the payoff nobody expects at day one.

What it teaches

Reflection (what happened, what mattered), expressive writing, emotional naming, daily discipline, and handwriting fluency that grows one honest page at a time.

Words to learn

journalentryreflectheadlinefeelingprivacyhabitdiarypage

Say this to your child

“"Journaling club! This notebook is yours — nobody reads it, ever. Three lines: today I saw, today I felt, tomorrow I hope. Spelling does not matter here. What was today’s headline?"”

Step by step

  1. Choose the notebook with full ceremony — the writer owns it; the family promises not to read it.
  2. Learn the starter: today I saw / today I felt / tomorrow I hope — three lines, two minutes, done.
  3. The no-spelling announcement: this notebook is about truth, not spelling — invented spellings are welcome and permanent policy.
  4. Headline game on big days: if today were a newspaper, what is the headline? — one dramatic sentence counts as a full entry.
  5. Keep the appointment: same time daily for two weeks, then the habit carries itself — and the writer reads page one aloud to their future self someday.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the notebook lies open with the pen mid-page and the writer leaning in — the card shows the club’s honest posture: nobody performs for a private notebook.

Ask your child

"What are the three lines?" (saw, felt, hope) "Who reads your journal?" (nobody — that is the rule) "What was today’s headline?" "How does it feel to write a feeling down?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may tape ticket stubs in as exhibits, rate days with invented star systems, or write in code that only they can read — private notebooks develop private cultures.

Out in the real world

Authors, scientists, athletes and explorers all kept journals — most of history’s best diaries were written by people your age or barely older. The habit is the same at nine as at ninety.

Try it together

Journal jar: paper slips with starters (the funniest thing today, something I learned, a question I have) — draw one on empty-page days. The jar ends the blank-page problem forever.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the three starter lines?" "What is the spelling rule in the journal?" (spelling does not matter — truth does) "When is journal time?" (same time, every day)

This lesson pairs with the Journaling flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Lego — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the Lego club habit: bricks sorted before building, instructions followed once and then escaped from, and every finished model given one honest improvement.

What is this?

Lego club is construction time with the world’s favorite bricks — sorted builds, instruction builds and free builds. The card’s printed skills are Build & Create: following the plan and then inventing past it.

What does it mean?

The rebuild challenge carries the lesson: build the set by instructions (reading diagrams is real reading), take it apart, and build something new from the same pieces — the same bricks, a different idea, which is creativity in its most physical form.

What does the child need to know?

A pile of bricks (sorted loosely by color or type), one small set with instructions if available, a baseplate or table, and a shelf where finished builds live. A camera documents the best ones before they are recycled into new ideas.

Why this matters

Lego builds spatial reasoning, instruction-following, patience for small pieces and the finishing habit. The sort-first rule quietly teaches the engineering truth: organized materials build faster.

What it teaches

Spatial planning, fine-motor precision, diagram reading, structural problem-solving (why did the tower lean?), creative reuse, and completion pride.

Words to learn

buildsortbricksinstructionsbaseplaterebuildstructuregalleryimprove

Say this to your child

“"Lego club! Sort first — colors in piles, five minutes, go. Now build the set by the instructions... done? GOOD. Now take it apart and build something nobody has ever seen. Same bricks, new idea!"”

Step by step

  1. Sort first: five minutes sorting bricks by color or shape — organized piles build faster, every engineer agrees.
  2. Instruction build: one small set, built exactly as drawn — celebrate the diagram-reading as the real skill it is.
  3. The rebuild: take it apart and build something NEW from the same pieces — no instructions, one idea, twenty minutes.
  4. The stress test: bridges get one book placed on them gently — if it holds, the engineer explains the trick; if not, the rebuild teaches more.
  5. Gallery night: the best build goes on display with a name card and a photo — then and only then may the bricks return to the pile for tomorrow.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the bricks are stacked mid-build in four colors with the builder’s hand placing the next piece — the card is always caught during, never after, because building IS the club.

Ask your child

"Why do we sort before building?" (organized pieces build faster) "What did the stress test teach?" (wide bases hold, triangles strengthen) "What did you build from the same bricks the second time?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may sort bricks by size beyond all reason, build a working drawer from bricks, or narrate stress tests like an engineering documentary — builders go deep.

Out in the real world

Architects, engineers and toy designers all built with bricks first. Real engineering schools use the rebuild challenge — same parts, new idea — as a creativity exam.

Try it together

Blind-build swap: two players sit back to back with identical brick piles — one describes their build, the other tries to match it blind. Precision vocabulary meets construction; both players win or both rebuild.

Understanding check

Ask: "What comes first — build or sort?" (sort) "What is the rebuild rule?" (same bricks, new idea) "How does the stress test work?" (one gentle book on the bridge)

This lesson pairs with the Lego flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Martial Arts — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the martial arts habit at home: the bow, the ready stance, one three-move kata practiced slow, and the club’s first law — calm before power, always.

What is this?

Martial arts club is structured movement with respect built in — stances, blocks, strikes practiced with control. The card’s printed skills are Discipline & Strength: self-control and the body it builds. Real sparring belongs to real dojos with real teachers.

What does it mean?

The bow is the curriculum: respect opens every class and calms the student before movement. Slow practice builds the form; speed arrives later on its own — the opposite of how children usually want to learn, which is exactly why it works.

What does the child need to know?

Clear floor space, a mirror if available, loose clothes and bare feet. A grown-up approves any moves that involve contact (none here — the home version is partner-free and always controlled).

Why this matters

Martial arts build strength, balance, listening and impulse control — the last one is the quiet superpower. The belt system also teaches long-horizon progress: small skills, tested honestly, repeated for years.

What it teaches

Stance strength, controlled striking (speed with an off switch), balance, kata memory (sequences held in the body), and the calm-under-excitement discipline.

Words to learn

bowstanceblockstrikekatabeltdojocontroldiscipline

Say this to your child

“"Martial arts club! We bow first — feet together, small bow. Now ready stance... hold it. Block — punch — block, slow like honey. Again, quick like rain. Control is the whole art."”

Step by step

  1. Open with the bow: feet together, hands at the sides, small bow — say what it honors (the teacher, the space, yourself).
  2. Ready stance: feet apart, knees soft, fists guarded — hold for a slow ten-count.
  3. The home kata: block, punch, block — five times SLOW like honey, five times quick like rain; the mirror shows the difference.
  4. Balance kick practice: one slow front kick, held, returned to stance with the same control — five per side, no higher than the waist.
  5. Close with the bow and the club’s question: when is power useful? (only with control) — the answer IS the discipline.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the student bows with hands pressed and eyes calm, black belt tied neat — the card captured the moment before movement, which is where this sport keeps its secret: the calm IS the training.

Ask your child

"Show me the bow." "What is the ready stance?" "Which is harder — slow or fast practice? Why?" (slow — it builds the control) "When is power useful?" (only with control)

What your child can say or do

Your child may bow before entering the kitchen, run the kata during cartoons, or remind the family that calm comes first (they will) — the discipline leaks out of the dojo.

Out in the real world

Martial artists, stunt performers and soldiers all train slow-then-fast. Real dojos worldwide start beginners on exactly this stance-block-punch sequence — belts come later, control comes first.

Try it together

Sensei says: the martial version of Simon Says — block, punch, bow, stance — and the trap is moving when the command lacks the bow first. Listening trained at full attention.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me the bow and the ready stance." "Recite the home kata." (block, punch, block) "What is the club’s first law?" (calm before power)

This lesson pairs with the Martial Arts flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Nature Crafts — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the nature crafts habit: a walk with collecting eyes, the fallen-things-only rule, and one gallery project that turns today’s pockets into tonight’s art.

What is this?

Nature crafts club is making with gathered materials — leaves, twigs, petals, stones — where the printed skills are Collect & Create: foraging with care and building with what the path offered.

What does it mean?

The gathering rule (only what has fallen) teaches early ecology: the leaf on the ground is finished; the leaf on the tree is working. Materials chosen by a walk carry stories — this leaf came from the big tree by the gate — which makes the art autobiographical.

What does the child need to know?

A collecting bag or basket per walker, glue, card or paper, and eyes that notice. Pressed flowers need heavy books; stone creatures need nothing but balance and a flat shelf.

Why this matters

Nature crafts build observation (what changed on the path?), fine-motor construction and seasonal awareness — the calendar arrives through materials. It also gets the family walking, which no other craft club can claim.

What it teaches

Observation walks, material discrimination (which leaf? why?), gluing and arrangement precision, seasonal vocabulary, and the leave-no-trace ethic.

Words to learn

collectgatherfallenpressarrangetextureseasongalleryhabitat

Say this to your child

“"Nature crafts club! Rules first: only fallen things, take a few, leave the path tidy. Walk and gather... now sort by color. This red leaf — from the crooked tree, remember? It is becoming an owl tonight."”

Step by step

  1. Set the gathering rules: fallen things only, take few from each spot, and leave the path as tidy as found.
  2. The noticing walk: ten minutes, pockets and bag filling — narrate the best finds by their stories (the red leaf from the crooked tree).
  3. Sort the haul at home by type and color — the arrangement IS the first design decision.
  4. Build the gallery: leaf-owl (big leaf body, twig legs, stone eyes), twig-star, petal-rainbow — glue to card, one creature or pattern per card.
  5. The exhibition: cards displayed on one wall, each titled with where its materials were found — the art now carries the walk inside it.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the collage holds a red leaf body and a small painted bird with a twig — the maker held the artwork up to the light, which is how nature crafts are always premiered.

Ask your child

"What is the gathering rule?" (fallen things only) "Where did each find come from?" (the story is the label) "Which season gave us these materials?" "What will the path offer next month?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may keep a finds drawer, press petals in every heavy book in the house, or refuse to walk anywhere without a bag — collectors become naturalists.

Out in the real world

Botanical illustrators, land artists and museum curators all collect and arrange from nature. The great land-art works are exactly this club, scaled up and photographed.

Try it together

Season swap: in autumn gather leaves, in winter gather evergreen sprigs and interesting shadows (trace them), in spring petals, in summer seeds — the club never closes, it changes costume.

Understanding check

Ask: "May we pick leaves from the tree?" (no — fallen only) "What sorts the haul before building?" (type and color) "What goes in each card’s title?" (where the materials were found)

This lesson pairs with the Nature Crafts flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Photography — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the photography club habit: look before shooting, hold with two hands, and end every session by choosing the keepers — because editing is the secret half of the art.

What is this?

Photography club is picture-making with any camera — framing, light noticing and the weekly selection ritual. The card’s printed skills are Observe & Create: seeing carefully and keeping what was seen.

What does it mean?

Photography teaches selection: the camera keeps everything, the photographer keeps one. The frame-first habit (decide what the picture is ABOUT before clicking) upgrades shots immediately — and the print-and-caption ritual turns snapshots into stories.

What does the child need to know?

Any phone or tablet camera (the club does not need gear), a list of five photo challenges, and a wall or album for the weekly keeper. Steady surfaces help; elbows-in technique helps more.

Why this matters

Photography builds observation, composition sense and narrative choice — and it feeds every other interest: the bug hunter photographs bugs, the baker photographs bakes. The keepers ritual also teaches editing judgment early.

What it teaches

Composition (subject placement, the rule of thirds in kid terms), steady-hand technique, light awareness, selection judgment, and caption writing that tells the story.

Words to learn

framesubjectfocuslightsteadyshotkeepercaptionalbum

Say this to your child

“"Photography club! Frame first — what is the picture ABOUT? Say it, then click. Two hands, elbows in, breathe... and the five-photo hunt begins: something red, something tiny, something funny!"”

Step by step

  1. Frame-first drill: before any click, say what the picture is about — THIS is a photo of the sleeping cat — then take it.
  2. Steady-shot school: two hands, elbows in, breath in and hold — five practice shots of the same object, keep the steadiest.
  3. The five-photo hunt: something red, something tiny, something funny, something from below, something that shows today — hunt, shoot, return.
  4. The selection: review all shots together and pick ONE keeper each — say WHY it won (the light, the moment, the story).
  5. Print or album the keepers with captions: one sentence per photo, writer’s words — the wall gallery grows weekly and tells the family’s real story.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the camera is held up with the lens at eye level and both hands steady — the card shows the club’s form: the photographer looks THROUGH the picture before taking it.

Ask your child

"What is this photo about — say it before clicking." "Why did this one win?" (the keeper question) "What does a caption do?" (tells the story the picture started) "What is on the hunt list today?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may photograph the same pet forty times (a series!), build caption libraries, or assign the family official-photographer badges — the wall gallery fills fast.

Out in the real world

Photojournalists, wildlife photographers and every family album run on this skill. Newspapers teach journalists the same rule: know what the picture is about before you raise the camera.

Try it together

Same-subject series: one object photographed five ways — close, far, from above, from below, in shadow — then the family votes on which tells the truth best. Perspective becomes visible.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we say before clicking?" (what the photo is about) "Show me the steady-hold." "What happens to the keeper?" (print, caption, wall)

This lesson pairs with the Photography flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Poetry — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the poetry club habit: one short poem per session, words chosen like colors, and the proud out-loud reading that turns writing into performance.

What is this?

Poetry club is small-writing with big permission — list poems, sound poems and metaphor games on one page. The card’s printed skills are Words & Feelings: exact word choices and the emotions they carry.

What does it mean?

Poetry teaches economy: five lines can hold a whole feeling, so every word must work. The list-poem starter removes the blank-page fear (the structure is given; the feelings fill it), and metaphor play teaches comparison — the engine of all creative writing.

What does the child need to know?

Paper, a pencil, and one good reading voice. A poetry book nearby for borrowing courage. Nothing needs to rhyme — announce this rule first; it frees every poet at the table.

Why this matters

Poetry builds vocabulary precision, emotional literacy and reading-aloud courage — and it is the shortest path to loving words: small poems win fast, and winning makes writers.

What it teaches

Word-choice precision, emotional naming, metaphor thinking, line-break awareness, and the performance voice that reads its own work with pride.

Words to learn

poemlineverserhyme (optional)metaphorimagerecitefeelingdraft

Say this to your child

“"Poetry club! First rule: poems do NOT have to rhyme. Now — the moon is a... pancake! The rain is a... drum solo! Now write yours: five lines, any feelings. And tonight we read them LOUD."”

Step by step

  1. Read one short poem aloud — just to hear what poems sound like in the room.
  2. The list-poem starter: five lines, given beginnings — I like / I wonder / I remember / I dream / I wish.
  3. The metaphor game: the moon is a... (pancake, nightlight, coin), the rain is a... — five quick rounds, no wrong answers, biggest laughs win.
  4. Write one real poem: any form, any subject, five lines maximum — and read it silently once to hear it.
  5. The reading: every poet reads aloud with the biggest voice in the house, audience snaps fingers (poetry applause) — and the poem goes on the wall.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the poet holds the notebook low and the free hand is already gesturing mid-recital — the card shows the club’s secret: poems are written alone but finished out loud.

Ask your child

"Which line of your poem feels strongest?" "What did the metaphor game teach about the moon?" "How does the audience applaud at poetry readings?" (finger snaps) "What feeling needs a poem next?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may write odes to the refrigerator, carry the notebook everywhere, or demand poetry readings after dinner — poets recruit audiences young.

Out in the real world

Song lyrics, commercials, speeches and greeting cards all use poetry’s tools. The metaphor game is a real writers’-room warm-up — late-night comedy shows play it every morning.

Try it together

Pass-the-poem: one line written, paper passed, next player adds a line, five players later the poem is read in full — collaborative nonsense that occasionally lands on something true.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is poetry’s first rule?" (it does not have to rhyme) "Give me one metaphor for the rain." "How long is tonight’s poem?" (five lines or fewer — every word works)

This lesson pairs with the Poetry flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Pottery — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the pottery club habit: one ball of clay, the oldest trick in the book (pinch pot), and the patience rules that carry the bowl from mud to cupboard.

What is this?

Pottery club is forming with clay — pinch pots, coil pots and small sculptures that dry into real objects. The card’s printed skills are Shape & Imagine: working the material and picturing it finished.

What does it mean?

Clay teaches revision without erasing: squashed and reformed is how clay works, which makes it the friendliest failure material in the house. The drying rule (slow, even, patient) adds the club’s signature lesson — the last step of making is waiting.

What does the child need to know?

Air-dry clay (the kindest starter — no kiln needed), a smooth table, a small bowl of water for cracking edges, and a shelf where works dry undisturbed. Hands are the only tools required.

Why this matters

Pottery builds hand strength, 3-D thinking and patience — and it produces OBJECTS: a bowl that holds keys, a cup that holds pencils. Functional art is the most convincing art a child can make.

What it teaches

Hand and finger strength, wall-thickness judgment, 3-D spatial planning, revision confidence (reshape is allowed), and drying patience.

Words to learn

claypinchcoilwallbasesmoothdrykiln (someday)glaze (someday)

Say this to your child

“"Pottery club! Warm the clay first — roll it like dough. Now the thumb goes in... pinch and TURN, pinch and turn — watch the bowl grow out of the ball! On the shelf it dries. Hands off — patience, potter."”

Step by step

  1. Warm the clay: roll it, squeeze it, get to know the lump — cold clay needs a minute of friendship.
  2. The pinch pot: push a thumb into the ball’s center, then pinch and TURN, pinch and turn — walls thin evenly, cracks get a wet finger.
  3. Coil pot two: roll snakes, stack them in rings, smooth the seams — the second ancient method, twice as tall.
  4. Name the piece and set it to dry on the shelf — the rule: hands off until fully dry, which takes days and builds the patience muscle.
  5. The debut: the dried pot holds something real — keys, pencils, hair ties — and dinner uses the pinch pot for salt. Functional from day one.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the potter’s hands shape a tall vessel on a spinning wheel — the wheel is the club’s someday-goal; today’s pinch pot uses the same truth: even walls, patient turning.

Ask your child

"Which way do we turn while pinching?" (slowly, a little at a time) "What fixes a crack?" (a wet finger) "How long does drying take?" (days — that is the rule) "What will your pot hold when it is done?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may build a whole dinner service, test whether the pot holds water (it teaches more than any lecture), or gift the first pot to a grandparent — potters produce keepers.

Out in the real world

Potters, ceramicists and dentists (crown molds!) all shape soft material into permanent forms. Archaeologists read whole civilizations from pot shards — your shelf is a future dig site.

Try it together

Pottery shop: dried works get price tags and a shop display; family members shop with play money and leave reviews — the economy of making things people want.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me the pinch-and-turn." "What fixes cracks?" (wet finger) "What is the drying rule?" (hands off until dry) "Where does the finished pot live?" (in use — holding something real)

This lesson pairs with the Pottery flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Puppetry — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the puppetry club habit: a puppet built from a sock, a voice invented in five minutes, and a doorway stage where shy performers become bold lions.

What is this?

Puppetry club is character building plus performance — making the puppet, finding its voice, and staging small shows from behind a sheet. The card’s printed skills are Create & Perform: building the character and bringing it alive.

What does it mean?

The puppet does the brave thing while the maker hides — which is why puppetry is the confidence club in disguise. The voice workshop (high, low, growly, fast) trains vocal control, and the two-scene rule (hello, joke, goodbye) teaches show structure.

What does the child need to know?

One sock or paper bag per puppet, buttons or paper eyes, glue or tape, a sheet for the stage (a doorway holds it with tape), and one audience. A puppet box grows naturally from here.

Why this matters

Puppetry builds crafting skills, voice control, improvisation and performance nerve with zero eye contact — the gentlest stage there is. It also produces the family’s permanent comedians.

What it teaches

Craft construction, vocal character work (pitch, speed, catchphrase), improvisation, show structure, and the behind-the-scenes teamwork of stagehands and puppeteers.

Words to learn

puppetstagevoicecharacterscript (optional)showbowaudienceperform

Say this to your child

“"Puppetry club! Build your character — eyes, hair, name. Now the voice: high? low? growly? Give it one catchphrase... and rehearse the entrance. The sheet goes up tonight — the show is ON!"”

Step by step

  1. Build the puppet: sock hand, eyes glued, hair from yarn — the maker decides everything, and names the character.
  2. The voice workshop: try three voices — high, low, growly — and pick the one the puppet keeps forever (plus one catchphrase).
  3. Rehearse the character walk: how does the lion peek over the stage edge? Practice the entrance; entrances are half the show.
  4. Hang the doorway stage: sheet across a doorway, knees behind, puppets peeking — the theater is open.
  5. The debut: two scenes, hello-joke-goodbye, audience applauds, puppets take a bow (puppets bow lower — it is tradition).

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the lion puppet sits up on the hand, mouth open mid-roar, and the puppeteer grins beside it — the card shows both halves of the club: the puppet performs, the person beams.

Ask your child

"What is your puppet’s catchphrase?" "Which voice won — high, low or growly?" "How does a puppet enter a show?" (peeking up over the stage) "What does the audience do at the end?" (applauds — and the puppets bow)

What your child can say or do

Your child may build a puppet family, run bedtime shows for siblings, or write the lion’s memoir (puppets have backstories) — theaters multiply in doorways.

Out in the real world

Puppeteers, animators and voice actors all started with a character on a hand. The Muppets, the West End’s Lion King, every cartoon voice — the training ground is identical.

Try it together

Puppet interview show: one puppet hosts, other puppets are guests with ridiculous jobs — the host asks five questions. Improvisation trained at full silliness.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name your puppet and its catchphrase." "Where does the stage hang?" (the doorway) "What are the two scenes?" (hello-joke and goodbye) "Who bows at the end?" (the puppets — lower, tradition)

This lesson pairs with the Puppetry flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Robotics — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the robotics club habit: robots spotted in the wild, instructions tested on human robots, and one build-invent-test loop run with bricks or kits.

What is this?

Robotics club is building machines that act — from brick robots with jobs to programmable kits when ready. The card’s printed skills are Build & Invent: constructing the machine and dreaming its next job.

What does it mean?

Robotics is the loop made physical: design, build, test, improve — and the test almost always fails first, which is the education. Spotting household robots (dishwasher, vacuum, washing machine) reframes the home as a robot zoo.

What does the child need to know?

Building bricks or any construction kit, a blindfold for the human-robot game, open floor space, and (later) any beginner programmable robot kit. Curiosity is the main component.

Why this matters

Robotics builds engineering logic, debugging patience and the machine-empathy of programming — plus the career-shaped discovery that machines do what we DESIGN, not what we wish.

What it teaches

Design thinking, construction skill, testing discipline, instruction precision, and the invent-what-is-needed habit (what job does this machine do?).

Words to learn

robotsensorprogramtestloopjobdesignimproveengineer

Say this to your child

“"Robotics club! First: robot spotting — the dishwasher is a robot, the toaster is a robot... now YOU are my robot: two steps forward, quarter turn left... CRASH. Debug the program, try again!"”

Step by step

  1. Robot spotting: name five robots in the house and their jobs — dishwasher (wash), vacuum (clean), washing machine (spin), toaster (brown), the child’s nightlight (glow).
  2. The human-robot course: one player is blindfolded, the other gives exact commands — two steps, quarter turn left, stop — to reach the teddy. Precision tested at walking speed.
  3. Debrief the crashes: which command failed? Rewrite the program and run it again — debugging with bodies.
  4. Design-and-build: sketch a robot with a real job (feeds the cat, sorts socks), then build it from bricks — sensor dots for eyes, moving parts discussed.
  5. The test: does it do the job in pretend-play? One improvement noted for version two — robots ship unfinished, that is the industry.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the robot stands with a heart on its chest and the builder beside it — the heart is the design brief: every robot is built for something someone cares about.

Ask your child

"What is the robot’s job?" (every design starts here) "What failed in the test?" (the debug question) "What improves in version two?" "Which house robot works hardest?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may program siblings for chores, design a homework robot (the family supports this dream), or narrate the dishwasher cycle like mission control — engineers spot systems.

Out in the real world

Robotics engineers, automation designers and Mars rover teams all run the same loop: design, build, test, improve. The Mars rovers are exactly this club, farther away.

Try it together

Robot job fair: each player presents a built robot with one job, one sensor and one flaw — the audience hires their favorite. Presenting inventions is half of engineering.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name three house robots and their jobs." "What is the design loop?" (design, build, test, improve) "What did your robot’s test fail at?" (and what fixed it)

This lesson pairs with the Robotics flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Science — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the science club habit: predictions written before testing, a sink-or-float census with ten suspects, and the notebook that turns kitchen games into real experiments.

What is this?

Science club is question-and-test time — predictions, experiments, observations and honest results. The card’s printed skills are Explore & Experiment: curiosity in the field and careful tests at the bench (kitchen counter).

What does it mean?

The write-your-guess-first rule is the whole scientific method in one habit: a prediction that is written down cannot quietly rewrite itself after the result. Wrong guesses are celebrated loudly — they mean the experiment taught something.

What does the child need to know?

A notebook (the lab journal), a sink or bowl of water, ten small waterproof objects, a pencil, and the family rule: everyone guesses BEFORE each object lands. Optional: a magnifying glass for field exploration.

Why this matters

Science builds prediction discipline, observation, honest recording and the resilience of being wrong in public — the exact skills every real lab runs on. It also answers the why-questions with experiments instead of lectures.

What it teaches

Prediction and hypothesis habits, observation detail, recording discipline (dated entries), result-vs-guess comparison, and curiosity that survives being wrong.

Words to learn

predictexperimentobserveresultrecordhypothesissinkfloatevidence

Say this to your child

“"Science club! Rule one: guess BEFORE we test — write it down, no changing. The orange: sink or float? ... Everyone voted? Then in it goes! A SURPRISE — that is a star in the journal!"”

Step by step

  1. Set the rule of the club: guess first, write it down, then test — no exceptions, even for scientists who are sure.
  2. The sink-or-float census: ten objects on the table — everyone votes sink or float on paper before each lands in the water.
  3. Record results in the lab journal: object, guess, result, and a star for every surprise — surprises are the club’s currency.
  4. The why hunt: pick the biggest surprise (the orange that floats WITH its peel, sinks without) and design one follow-up test together.
  5. Field exploration: one magnifying-glass walk — observe three things closely and one question goes home in the journal for next time.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the scientist holds the magnifying glass to one eye and the flask of green liquid in the other hand — one eye on the evidence, one hand on the test: the club’s whole posture.

Ask your child

"What is the rule of the club?" (guess first, then test) "Which result surprised us most?" "What should we test next — and what is your guess?" "Why do we write results down?" (so they can be checked — and so surprises get stars)

What your child can say or do

Your child may test everything in the house for floatability (guard the phone), keep the lab journal like a treasure log, or predict weather with sudden authority — scientists generalize.

Out in the real world

Chemists, marine biologists, doctors and quality testers all run on guess-test-record. The surprise-star system is how real labs treat anomalies: the weird result is the interesting one.

Try it together

Mystery box: one sealed box with an object inside — five allowed tests (shake, weigh by hand, tilt, listen, smell) and then a written guess before opening. Evidence before revelation.

Understanding check

Ask: "What comes first, guess or test?" (guess — written down) "What do we star in the journal?" (surprises) "Show me the follow-up test we designed." (and its result)

This lesson pairs with the Science flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Skateboarding — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the skateboarding club habit safely: gear on before anything rolls, stance learned on carpet where the board cannot move, and surfaces climbed in order — carpet, grass, pavement.

What is this?

Skateboarding club is board time with a ladder — stance, pushes, glides and safe falling, practiced surface by surface. The card’s printed skills are Balance & Confidence: staying over the board and getting back on after every tumble.

What does it mean?

The surface ladder is the method: carpet (board still, body learns stance), grass (board rolls slowly, falls are soft), pavement (real riding). Each rung adds exactly one new variable — the way confidence is actually built, one honest step at a time.

What does the child need to know?

A skateboard, a helmet (level, strapped — the ritual stands), knee and elbow pads, flat safe ground, and the falling rules: crouch low, roll on pads, never stiff-arm. A grown-up walks the first pavement sessions.

Why this matters

Skateboarding builds balance, persistence and the specific bravery of trying again after falling — the sport’s whole culture is built on the get-back-on. It also teaches equipment respect: gear is part of the identity.

What it teaches

Dynamic balance, pushing technique, braking (foot drag), falling safely, and the retry muscle that skateboarders carry into everything else.

Words to learn

stancepushglidefoot brakepadshelmetfallrollretry

Say this to your child

“"Skateboarding club! Gear first — helmet, pads, falling rules recited. Now carpet stance: feet over the bolts, knees soft... rock with me. Grass push next — tiny rolls. Pavement is EARNED."”

Step by step

  1. Gear ritual first: helmet level and strapped, pads on knees and elbows — recite the falling rules together before the board ever moves.
  2. Carpet stance: board on the rug, feet over the bolts, knees bent — rock side to side until the stance is home. The board cannot move; the body learns.
  3. Grass push: board on grass or thick carpet, one foot pushes gently, the other rides — tiny rolls, tiny balance, soft ground below.
  4. Pavement glide: flat smooth ground, one gentle push, both feet over the bolts, eyes forward — glides counted in seconds like flight time.
  5. The foot brake: back foot drags low and slow to stop — rehearsed ten times before speed exists. Then the session ends with the retry rule: every fall earns one more try.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the board stands upright in one hand with the rider dressed and grinning — the card shows the club’s rhythm: half of skateboarding is walking with your board, planning the next try.

Ask your child

"Recite the falling rules." (crouch, roll, never stiff-arm) "Where do our feet go?" (over the bolts) "What is the foot brake?" (back foot drags low) "What does every fall earn?" (one more try)

What your child can say or do

Your child may sleep with the board, count glides like flight hours, or teach younger kids carpet stance on day one — skaters pass the ladder down.

Out in the real world

Skateboarders, surfers and snowboarders share this balance training. Every famous skater started on carpet in a living room — the surface ladder is the sport’s real history.

Try it together

Glide olympics: longest glide, straightest line between two marks, smoothest foot-brake stop — three events, medals mandatory, and the retry rule applies to the podium poses too.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me carpet stance." "Name the surface ladder." (carpet, grass, pavement) "How do we stop?" (foot brake — low and slow) "What does a fall earn?" (one more try)

This lesson pairs with the Skateboarding flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Table Tennis — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the table tennis habit: grip first, cooperative rallies second — the family chases its own record instead of each other, and everyone’s game improves.

What is this?

Table tennis club is paddle time at any table with a net (or a books-and-string net) — serves, rallies and the record chase. The card’s printed skills are React & Play: fast eyes and the love of the rally.

What does it mean?

Cooperative counting (how many consecutive hits can WE keep going?) beats competitive scoring for beginners: nobody loses points, everybody watches the ball better. Small swings win — the table is close and the ball is light.

What does the child need to know?

Two paddles, a handful of balls, a table with any net (a row of books works), and clear space for backswings. The record sheet taped to the wall is the club’s trophy.

Why this matters

Table tennis builds reaction speed, hand-eye coordination and focus — often cited as the fastest-reaction ball sport. It is also the most weatherproof club in the school: the whole league fits in the garage.

What it teaches

Reaction speed, tracking a fast small object, paddle control, serve consistency, and the cooperative mindset of building a shared record.

Words to learn

rallyservepaddlenetbouncespinrecordpointreturn

Say this to your child

“"Table tennis club! Shake hands with your paddle — ten bounces, steady... now the rally: one bounce each side, GENTLE. Count out loud with me — how high can WE go? The record sheet is waiting!"”

Step by step

  1. Grip school: shake hands with the paddle — firm fingers, relaxed wrist — and practice ten gentle bounces on the paddle face.
  2. The bounce ladder: ten bounces flat, five bounces alternating paddle sides — control before the net is involved.
  3. Serve basics: ball tossed, paddle meets it after the bounce, one bounce each side — five serves each, no score, all practice.
  4. The cooperative rally: hit back and forth gently — one bounce on each side — counting aloud; the family record goes on the wall sheet.
  5. The record chase: three rally attempts per session, the best count written down — the record exists to be broken together, and the sheet tells the story of the month.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the player’s paddle is up and the eyes lock forward — the card shows the club’s real skill: the eyes arrive before the paddle, always.

Ask your child

"How do we hold the paddle?" (shake hands with it) "What are we counting?" (consecutive hits — together) "What happened to today’s record?" "Why small swings?" (the table is close and the ball is light)

What your child can say or do

Your child may practice paddle bounces during cartoons, demand the record sheet be laminated, or serve underhand until it clicks — the record chase keeps everyone honest.

Out in the real world

Table tennis champions, video gamers and surgeons all train reaction speed. The sport is an Olympic event with a living-room footprint — the cheapest elite training there is.

Try it together

Around-the-table doubles: after each hit, players run one place around the table — chaos, laughter and reaction training in one rule. The rally count still counts.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me the paddle grip." "What are we chasing?" (the family rally record) "How big are the swings?" (small — control wins)

This lesson pairs with the Table Tennis flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Tennis — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the tennis club habit: the racket-control ladder before any court, a bench as the first net, and the handshake finish that defines the sport’s manners.

What is this?

Tennis club is racket-and-ball time — control drills, mini-nets, serves and small matches. The card’s printed skills are Move & Compete: covering ground and playing to win with grace.

What does it mean?

Tennis point-by-point trains reset thinking: the last ball is finished, the next ball is a new game — a skill adults pay coaches to teach. The control ladder (bounces, edges, walking) builds the racket feel that every court skill borrows.

What does the child need to know?

One racket, a few balls, a wall or bench for the first net, and shoes that run. Real courts come later; the driveway runs the whole beginner program.

Why this matters

Tennis builds running, timing and the emotional habit of playing hard and shaking hands after — the sport literally stops for a handshake. It is also a lifetime game: the skills learned at six work at sixty.

What it teaches

Racket control, timing and contact point, footwork (small steps), serve basics, and the competitive-with-manners mindset.

Words to learn

racketserverallynetbaselinevolleycourtpointhandshake

Say this to your child

“"Tennis club! The ladder first: ten flat bounces, ten on the edge, ten while walking... now the wall — it never misses, keep up! And every match ends at the net: handshake, win or lose."”

Step by step

  1. The racket-control ladder: ten flat bounces, ten edge bounces, ten while walking — the ladder climbs each session.
  2. Wall tennis: hit the ball to the wall and let it bounce back — one bounce, hit again; the wall never misses, which trains everything.
  3. Bench-net rallies: a bench as the net, underhand serves, cooperative counting like table tennis — the record chase transfers.
  4. The footwork drill: small steps between shots — shuffle, shuffle, hit, recover — big lunges are for emergencies only.
  5. The first mini-match: first to four points, underhand serves only — and the match ends at the net with a real handshake, win or lose, every time.
