Look closer at the picture

On the card, the racket is held in front with both hands ready and the eyes forward — the card shows the ready position, which is where tennis players live between every shot.

Ask your child

"Show me the ready position." "What does the ladder train?" (racket control) "Where does every match end?" (at the net — handshake) "What do small steps do that big lunges do not?" (arrive on time, recover faster)

What your child can say or do

Your child may run the ladder during TV time, play wall tennis for an hour (the wall is patient), or referee sibling matches with full ceremony — the handshake ritual sticks hard.

Out in the real world

Tennis champions, coaches and every Saturday club player run on racket control and reset thinking. The handshake rule is enforced at Wimbledon — it is the sport’s signature.

Try it together

Court math: the score climbs 15, 30, 40, game — teach the weird scoring as a counting song, and let the child referee a family match with a chalk scoreboard. Math hides in the sport.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me ten racket bounces." "What is the first net?" (the bench) "How does every match end?" (handshake at the net) "Recite the score song." (15, 30, 40, game)

This lesson pairs with the Tennis flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.

CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Volunteering — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the volunteering club habit: one act of service a week, planned by the child, carried by the child, and finished with the delivery moment that makes helping real.

What is this?

Volunteering club is organized helping — donations, neighbor favors, cleanups and kindness projects. The card’s printed skills are Share & Support: giving time and lifting someone else’s week.

What does it mean?

Volunteering works best when the child picks the project (ownership) and finishes the delivery (completion): a toy carried into a donation center teaches more than a dozen lectures. The two-basket method makes giving visible — keep some, give some, choose honestly.

What does the child need to know?

Two baskets or boxes, a calendar for the kindness week, and one real destination — a donation bin, a neighbor’s door, a family member who needs a hand. Nothing needs buying.

Why this matters

Volunteering builds empathy into habit, gratitude by contrast, and the helper identity — the child who has carried a donation box treats community as theirs. It is also the club with the most transferable skill set: every workplace calls it teamwork.

What it teaches

Empathy and perspective-taking, planning and follow-through, service vocabulary, gratitude practice, and the completion pride of delivered help.

Words to learn

volunteerdonatecommunitydeliverkindnessneighborshareservegive

Say this to your child

“"Volunteering club! Two baskets today — KEEP and GIVE — and you make every choice. Which toys are ready to make someone else happy? ... And when the basket is full, YOU carry it. The carrying is the magic."”

Step by step

  1. The two-basket sort: toys and books into KEEP and GIVE baskets — the child makes every call, and the GIVE basket fills with real favorites, not rejects.
  2. The kindness calendar: one small act per day for a week — draw a picture for someone, help with a chore unasked, share a snack.
  3. The neighbor project: one helpful task for someone nearby — water plants while away, return a bin, deliver cookies — planned and scheduled by the child.
  4. The delivery: the child physically carries the GIVE basket or the cookies to the destination — the carrying is the moment the club exists for.
  5. The reflection: one journaling line — what did we give, how did it feel — and next week’s project gets chosen before the feeling fades.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the VOLUNTEER shirt is worn and the hand reaches out beside the donations box — the shirt is the invitation, and the open hand is the club’s whole method.

Ask your child

"What goes in the GIVE basket?" (favorites, not rejects — why?) "What did we deliver this week?" "How did the person react?" "What is next week’s project?" (chosen before the feeling fades)

What your child can say or do

Your child may refill the GIVE basket weekly, plan kindness calendars for the whole family, or wave at every delivery driver (community awareness is spreading) — volunteers multiply.

Out in the real world

Food banks, animal shelters, park cleanups and disaster relief all run on volunteers — most start exactly this young. The two-basket sort is a real donation-center ritual.

Try it together

Kindness bingo: a five-square card — help a sibling, thank a worker, give a toy, make a card, check on a neighbor — completed in one week, celebrated loudly, then drawn fresh.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the two baskets?" (KEEP and GIVE) "What is the delivery rule?" (the child carries it) "Name this week’s kindness calendar act." (and how it landed)

This lesson pairs with the Volunteering flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.
